author: @bloody_albatross
text:
59:50 The thing about Qt is that it was first created before there was the C++ STL or before it was widely available in compilers. That meant they implemented a lot of the standard things themselves (QString, QList, QPointer, ...). And because that all is a little bit different than the STL stuff Qt mostly kept their own stuff. Besides that it uses quite a few macros for their "signals and slots" and basically runtime reflection of QObjects. It's almost a dialect of C++. That said, Linus Torvalds, who famously hates C++, uses Qt in his hobby project. At first he used Gtk, but according to him that is so bad, he rather uses C++ (even a macro heavy magic C++ framework) just for the GUI rather than using Gtk. I think that says something about Qt.
[Edit: I was told it wasn't Linus who chose to port from Gtk to Qt. Haven't looked it up.]

This is the first time I've ever seen a popular C++ rant where it's clear the speaker is actually an expert in the language. There were a couple of nitpicks:

* inline functions, when they aren't inlined, are coalesced by the linker into a single symbol. static functions are the ones which are preserved in each TU via internal linkage semantics.
* RVO isn't an optimization, despite the name. It's a requirement of the language from the value category definitions. That's why it happens on -O0. prvalues don't create objects, there's nothing to copy.

author: @driedurchin
text:
As an ex-professional C++ developer, here's my small points of contention. I largely agree, but feel I must advocate:
1. Many of the IDE problems are not a thing with CLion, which supports MSVC projects
2. Uninitialized variables are now initialized by default with a compiler flag, with an opt in uninitialized attribute. Too little too late, but it is in the standard now.
3. There is something to be said for the incremental compilation benefits of the .h/.cpp split. It's marginal, but worth mentioning. Rust not having dynamic linking, and per-crate TUs is a pain point.
4. Some of the "the compiler allows this" arguments are weaker than others. Yes it's important to have sane defaults, but many many people are on the level about good warnings.
5. I won't tell you how to make a video, but if affecting change was your goal, a cooler tone would be easier to forward this video to someone on the standards committee
6. To be fair, SIMD support is pretty lacking everywhere in my experience
7. RVO is not technically a compiler optimization, it's standardized.
8. Async Rust is absolutely NOT harder than other languages. Having used Python asyncio and Rust with tokio to recently write the same program twice for work (two sides of a connection) what took me 40 minutes to get working (with proper cancellation and error handling) took me 6 hours in python to get working at all, let alone handling Ctrl+C. It's harder than sync Rust, and less ergonomic, but you can get correct code wildly fast.

One thing I'd add on is that there is a book about C++14 I think that said "Use these features now, use these features carefully, and NEVER touch these features". It was about an even 3 way split of the features...

Overall, I think the biggest issue in my mind is the notions of "there should be one obvious way to do things" and "sensible defaults" are the two biggest missing philosophies in the language.

Another angle to look at it that I feel was omitted is as follows: I would assert that the single largest miss-step in the language is governance. I don't think the poor design decisions were unavoidable consequences of age. I think had the language had a governance that did a better job of soliciting feedback from real users, instead of an exclusive, high-barrier-to-entry, committee, things could have gone different.

Fantastic video overall, just thought I'd leave my thoughts.

author: @julih4152
text:
just one thing I noticed: I think the section about the ABI and the lack of a package manager is a bit unfair, in my opinion. Comparing this to languages like C#, Python, and similar ones overlooks an important difference: all of those languages (with the exception of Rust) rely on some form of intermediate layer, such as a JIT compiler or an interpreter. That abstraction makes it much easier to build a package manager, since you don’t have to deal directly with OS and architecture-specific details at compile time.

Rust, while also not using an intermediate layer, is very restrictive in how software can be deployed. For example, distributing libraries in binary form is essentially not supported. If you attempt to do so, you lose the borrow checker guarantees at the API border and end up in an unsafe C-like situation - similar to how C++ makes use of the stable C ABI, as mentioned in the video. What also makes it way easier to manage packages.

Given these constraints, I think the comparison deserves a bit more nuance.

author: @ScorgRus
text: 52:25 begin() and end() do not "point to an element". They point to a boundary of an element, whether that element exists (constructed) there or not. In a contiguous memory block, where the elements are placed with no gaps in between, the right boundary of element i is the left boundary of element i+1. Therefore, end() points to the right boundary of the whole array (the last element, which may not exist). The choice of left/right element matters only for dereferencing. Respectively, rbegin() and rend() point to the right and left boundaries of an array (symmetric to begin/end).

author: @kyoai
text:
Some issues, I won't go through the entire video:
Random numbers: Why not use rand()%X instead? Yes, you can use the verbose example you gave, but that is only really needed if you want to customize the generator. I'm pretty sure Java or Python has similar customization options that would be equally verbose as your C++ example. And yes, rand() is from C, however C++ is mostly a superset of C, therefore rand() is also part of C++, same goes for printf(). If the task is merely to print a single message out, printf is more than enough and would be the more fair comparison.

New objects: Why are you comparing a normal allocation in Java with a unique_ptr in C++? unique_ptr has totally different purposes than a mere object allocation. If you use new operator, syntax-wise it's pretty much the same in Java and C++. Yes, it's less safe, but that was not the point you were making at that point.

Casts: There are many different casts because they are supposed to be used in different ways, ensuring you know what you're doing. Try emulating reinterpret_cast in Java to the same degree as what you can do in C++, it'll be a lot messier and verbose than just using it in C++.

Not saying that you are completely wrong in every point, and in several parts I agree with you, however when you want to compare languages you also have to make sure you are comparing the two languages fairly. I could turn this easily around and write verbose Java- or Python code and compare it with an equivalent one-liner in C++: "Omagawd, you need to declare an entire class in Java just to have a main function AND you need to explicitly mark it public static, that is so verbose for a simple Hello World, while in C++ you only have to write a simple global main function, clearly C++ is better".

author: @TranscendentBen
text:
1:15:04 I saw this 'problem' circa 1986 when first learning C. All the how-to-C books showed programs starting with prototypes of all functions used at the start of the source file, then the body of main() and finally the bodies of the functions. I had already learned Pascal years earlier which traditionally has each function body defined before usage, then main at the bottom of the file. I eventually figured out you could do the same with C, put main at the end and you'd only need prototypes for external or recursive functions. I was quite annoyed at the textbooks claiming to teach C.

Having learned assembly back then, I understood that this was to help the compiler build the symbol table by defining something before it's used, to reduce the number of passes and make assembly/compilation faster. Nowadays computers are (orders of magnitude) faster but we have other ways of slowing down compilation (you already mentioned having whole libraries in include files - I've use BOOST, it's quite effective at slowing compilation).

text: i have never been so stressed from watching a video before

30:45 : C++ 11 was not the first use of the term "Modern C++". The oldest one I know of is "Modern C++ Design" from 2001. That is not just an incidental use in the title but it apparently popularized the term to contrast with C style C++. I'm not very familiar with it, but when I learned of C++ in school, they clarified that at that time, which was just before C++ 11 IIRC, the term "modern C++" already could be referring to things that were 10 years out of date, and was already a significant problem and source of confusion.

9:56 There's actually more fundamental problem about the naming of the vector. Anyone who has basic knowledge about the concept of vector in mathematics would think they are immutable by default and do not change in its size. You don't really append, prepend, remove, or do whatever mutate the original vector in mathematics or physics. Instead you create another vector which contains the original vector (or vice versa). However, vector in C++ is mutable, which is unusual in mathematics. 

Also, people usually would associate vectors with operations such as cross product, dot product, addition, subtraction. std::vector, however, does not come with such operations, which leads confusion for beginners who don't know it's just another term for arrays that can grow at runtime. Though I haven't looked such libraries, I'm almost certain that either designers of linear algebra libraries on C++ had hard time choosing another suitable name, or users of them spend a lot of time figuring out what it refers to every time they see the identifier 'vector' (or go verbose by prepending namespace).

I'm really sad that Rust took this nonsensical legacy of C++ which was just a result of pure laziness of the original STL authors. They could have taken better names like DynArray or ArrayList, as Java did.

author: @jfolz
text:
Re: Age of Rust libraries.

In any other language that I know, when looking for a library to use, I first check when it was last updated. An abandoned library is a time bomb. With Rust it's the opposite. A library with a well-defined scope is simply done at some point. Importantly, breaking changes in new editions do not break old code. An app written in Rust 2024 can use any library written in Rust 2015 without issue. Metadata instructs the compiler which edition of the language to use for each code unit. And naturally, someone made a library that lets you switch editions inside the same file XD

author: @scriber36
text:
To be fair out of the 3 usages of static mentioned, the first 2 is the same. It is a singular variable not instantiated; hence it persist across function calls and hence it exists not bound to any instance. The only difference is its scope; where you define it; and hence where it is accessible from.

(My personal opinion: static local variables is a cursed idea in high-level programming context.)

The 3rd usecase also fits the definition if you think about it. Using the definition "a singular thing accessible only from the containing scope"; if we consider the file a scope, then all the 3 use-cases fit this.

I'm not saying it is good design, but these are rather similar scenarios. And let's not forget C++ comes from C... where 'int' is specific to the hardware etc... it is very technical instead of "platform-idependently declarative"; static makes most sense when thinking about the C++ compiler - what it will do with the concepts marked static. Then they all are the same; a non-instantiated singular thing shared by the compilation unit, limited in access to where it was defined. That's it. That's static.

text: Pretty much 90% of C++'s mistakes can be attributed to it wanting to replace C and therefore having to be backwards compatible with C. Now let it be known that I haven't worked on large scale C or C++ programs; just hobby stuff in both languages, but it's largely been my experience that learning C felt like it was somewhat oudated and janky, yet made sense, and learning C++ felt like a moving target. If you think C++ was the worst programming language of all time, you certainly have never seen COBOL.
And I find it quite silly to compare C++ with Java and C# which have nearly the same syntax, but come with giant, commercial class libraries - as if support (and control) from a huge company was a feature of the language itself. Java and C# also target only a single instruction set, a single ABI, a single bit-width, and a cozy userspace... to run the programs on different architectures, you need a VM which - guess what - is written in C++. So these languages let C++ do the heavy lifting.

author: @NickBibassis
text:
I really liked the video for its attitude and words of wisdom, but some annoying generalizations like:
• Macs can't be upgraded - no different than the vast majority of PC ultrabooks
• Macs don't last - except for the butterfly keyboard saga, Macs are well known for durability and OS update support
Linux - I've used Linux for decades for personal and professional use alongside Windows desktop/server and macOS and I'm still blown away how difficult it can be to create something simple like a 802.1ad network connection because steps vary based on the Linux flavour and vintage.
Best way to run non-server Linux ? 
• A VM on a Mac or Windows workstation - snapshots are a beautiful way to undo what you, or an update, f'd up.
• Want to experiment? Clone the VM and feel free to blow it up and revert back to a working state in seconds. Bare metal Linux as a daily driver is asking for problems when things go sideways.

author: @AidanMcHendry-c6j
text: I'd just like to interject for a moment. What you’re referring to as Linux, is in fact, GNU/Linux, or as I’ve recently taken to calling it, GNU plus Linux. Linux is not an operating system unto itself, but rather another free component of a fully functioning GNU system made useful by the GNU corelibs, shell utilities and vital system components comprising a full OS as defined by POSIX. Many computer users run a modified version of the GNU system every day, without realizing it. Through a peculiar turn of events, the version of GNU which is widely used today is often called “Linux”, and many of its users are not aware that it is basically the GNU system, developed by the GNU Project. There really is a Linux, and these people are using it, but it is just a part of the system they use. Linux is the kernel: the program in the system that allocates the machine’s resources to the other programs that you run. The kernel is an essential part of an operating system, but useless by itself; it can only function in the context of a complete operating system. Linux is normally used in combination with the GNU operating system: the whole system is basically GNU with Linux added, or GNU/Linux. All the so-called “Linux” distributions are really distributions of GNU/Linux.

author: @MatthewStutzman-v1f
text:
Big tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft make money by locking users into their ecosystems. Once you depend on their operating system or messaging platform, they can control prices, compatibility, and what apps you’re allowed to use.

Linux and most open-source software avoid this problem because no single company owns them. They’re transparent, community-driven, and not designed to trap you.

Standardized open-source protocols—like SMS, email, USB, or Wi-Fi—are essential for real competition. They let different devices, apps, and operating systems talk to each other. Without open standards, any company could create a private protocol that only works inside its own ecosystem. That instantly kills competition because no rival product could communicate with your friends, coworkers, or devices. And once a company controls the standard, it can raise prices, limit features, or block alternatives without losing users.

We’re still early in the digital age, and we can choose between a future controlled by a few corporations or one built on open, interoperable systems. If you disagree, tell me why. If you agree, try Linux.

author: @dr.syedinayatullah9125
text:
Honestly, right now Linux just doesn’t seem like it will ever become suitable for common users.
I’ve tried many distros with a serious intention to switch, but as a teacher, I still can’t rely on it for daily work.
The biggest issue is Microsoft Office compatibility. Tools like LibreOffice, WPS Office, and OnlyOffice claim 95–99% compatibility, but that remaining 1% is exactly where problems happen—formatting breaks, formulas behave differently, or presentations lose their layout. For a teacher or student, that small mismatch creates constant doubt: will my file open correctly on someone else’s Windows system?
On top of that, there’s no proper Microsoft Office or OneNote support on Linux, which is a major limitation in education.
And even beyond Office, there’s always uncertainty. If I need a new application in the future, there’s no guarantee it will even exist on Linux.
Linux is powerful and great for programmers and technical users, no doubt. But for common users like students and teachers who need reliability and zero compatibility issues, it still doesn’t provide peace of mind.
This is just my honest experience after trying it seriously.

author: @SkyyySi
text:
C is NOT functional, it's procedural. Functional means that functions have no side effects, which is definitely not the case for C. Functional also implies other things, like First-Class-Functions, meaning you can pass them around just like any other data type, ie:

def f(af):
    return af(5) + 3


def g(x):
    return x * x


print(f(g)) # --> 28


EDIT: Also, in functional programming, a function can be created anonymously. If you define an int, for example, you would use a syntax like this:

myint: int = 69420

In a functional language, functions can also be created like this:

myfunc = lambda x: x//2 if x % 2 == 0 else x*3+1

This comes in useful when, for example, a function A takes another function B as a parameter, but you don't want to bind B to any function name.

Also, use C/C++ if you want high performance, properly structured code, not having to deal with 10 million classes, not having to create a class any time you want to do anything, learning operating systems, learning embedded systems, learning network systems, learning security systems, and even scripting if you're good enough - vim and fast fingers go a long, long way.

Don't learn C/C++ if you want to glue some code fragments together and hope it works. It'll suck your soul and joy like a Dementor. It'll make you want to rip pieces of your own flesh out just to balance out the psychological pain. It'll get inside your head and make your eyes bleed while spending hours parsing through those thousands of lines of code to find that shitty off by one that's generating your runtime error. It'll make you scream in agony when someone cracks your software open because you forgot to free a pointer or used a deprecated unsafe version of a string library. It'll fuck you up, heal you, and fuck you up again.

IMO these languages are the best languages. They provide both abstraction - you can implement OOP concepts in C if you're good enough to do it - and control - memory management, kernel calls, process execution, etc. You get fast speeds, you get proper syntax - so long having a line of code that fills up your whole screen - and you're pretty much forced to use best practices, principles and patterns - the other option is ripping your eyes out while figuring out why the hell 1 out of 3 runs generate a seemingly nonexistent segfault. These are not your standard find-a-lib-read-a-tutorial-glue-some-shit-together-there-you-go java-type languages. These are craft languages. They reward those that take the time to learn how stuff hows. To figure out how the compiler processes things. To understand how the linker manages resources. To deeply think about what's the best way to cut a corner and get that min-max optimization that will make your system 1ms faster on that particular function. On the other hand, they punish everyone who doesn't do that. Harshly. Terribly. They'll scream "WRONG!" in your face, and when you ask why the answer will be "STOOPID!". Very punitive. Very rewarding. Very fun.

And truth is, the world runs in C. Your OS runs in C. Your phone runs in C. Your browser, your server, your database, your router, your car, your toothbrush, your microwave. Everything. Even if it's not in C, you can code it in C. That's the beauty of it. That's why it's so hard. It's an art form in it's own right. Plus it'll make virtually any other language feel like pushing solids into shapes. It's wonderful - and highly addictive.

Then there's the culture. I've found that C coders are very ruthless, but very empathetic once they assert you're in it for the long run. The same person that gives a half backed sour answer will take their time to slowly guide you through the process if they feel you really want to learn, really want to master it. It's really a whole thing. Spiritual, even. Can't enter the Temple unless your heart is in the right place.

So yes. Access your goals, take your time, figure out how far down the rabbit hole you want to go, and if the answer is 1, you'll know.

author: @Adam_Lyskawa
text: It's not that C# is slower by itself. It uses the garbage collector that is slow, automatic memory allocation that can be slow in some cases. And it uses a framework instead of a kind of a standard library, that is not slow, but uses a lot of disk space and RAM. C# can be super fast in many applications, with the speed comparable to lower level languages. However, if you need real-time timing precision or low-level hardware access - it's no joy. Also GC can get in the way when you need smoothness, like in games. GC is good, but when you don't exactly control WHEN and how it happens, it could introduce annoying lags. BTW, C# is fast only with the latest .NET. 6.0 or newer. Best - compiled into native executable. Still, not yet any good for embedded - too bloated. Also, making C# code fast is not an easy task. You have countless ways to make anything very slow. BTW, pointers are not scary. Their magic is overrated. Think of them as normal references in C#. BTW, you can use pointers in C#. But it's pretty POINTLESS ;) JK, I actually found some uses, like processing the bitmaps for example. Most of the time you just don't need them.

The main source of being slower is the garbage collector (not a problem if you program carefully) and the built-in safety checks for things like array bounds (which you should be doing in C anyway unless you consider yourself perfect).

author: @homersimpson8955
text: Stereotypes aside, C is the simplest language from C, C++ and C#. You still need to know how to use it, but it very straight forward and was created to write recompiled OS, which was known as Unix. C is native for almost all OS currently running. C++ originally was compiled into C code and fully bases on C with additional features, some of them was essential, like classes. Other was disputable, like exceptions. Overall C++ has more features than C, so it obviously it more difficult to learn, but those features are useful to mantain big applications, so when you learnt C++, it's more easier to mantain the code, if you writing something big. You still can emulate classes with C, using dynamic libraries, but in C++ doing it in more essential way. I'm not very familiar with C#, so can't say much about it, but it definitely more complicated than C (especially library) and when it came out interpreter was extremely slow compare to compiled code. Yes, you can run interpreter on diffetent platforms and you no need to recompile the application, also you have a runtime features, which simply not possible with compiled code, due to interpreter, but it all came with additional cost in performance and recompiling your application is not an issue, when you know your target platforms. So, make your choise wisely and don't listen to stereotypes, the simplest to learn is C, and if you know how to use it with dynamic libraries, C is suitable for a big applications. C++ and C# are compatible with design patterns which may help or may not to build you better applications, but it's essentially the next step, after you understand how C works. :)

author: @GameDevNerd
text:
C# is _not_ "way slower", you're totally ignoring the nuances and complexity of performance and optimization, and the reality that sometimes C# is _faster_ at certain things. At scale, in enterprise development, C# is _crazy fast_ and stable if it's written by skilled programmers. No one would use it for games, for example, if it couldn't be fast enough to make games as performant as C++ can. I'm actually writing an engine with C# targeting DirectX 12. My C# code will absolutely smoke the average developer's equivalent in C or C++ ...

Also, C is _not_ "functional" just because it calls its routines "functions", that's just a name they slapped on the feature ... C is imperative/procedural and structural. Functional languages are languages like Lisp, Haskell, F#, etc ... _completely_ different type of programming paradigm.

author: @BumHaven
text: I could not agree more. As someone who started programming in 1993, my first languages were C and a bit of Assembly. Over the course of my career I have developed significant commercial projects in C/C++, Objective-C, Java, Javascript and Python. Platforms spanned win16 / win32 API development on Windows, Objective-C w/WebObjects / EOF on NeXT / OpenStep followed by full stack web and iOS Developer development. Early in my career I agonized over every line of code trying to make it "perfect".  There is a better way. Avoid perfection and just code as much as possible, ideally on projects that interest you. Once a project is complete, then look back and figure out what you could have done better. Share what you have done with people you respect and get their feedback. Take those lessons and move on to the next project.

Keep shit straight forward. And keep shit CONSISTENT. After you finish touching a file nobody should be able to tell that you bolted on new functionality. It should blend in as if it was always there.  Knowledge of weird C++ tricks doesn't really help you in the industry. What really matters in a professional setting is quick code navigation/comprehension and good communication skills. That's it.

author: @stea27
text:
Well said. I also agree that it is much more important to achieve your goal, than to struggle or even give up midway because you can't do it the way some group of people want.  In time, you'll definitely learn what is good practice, what is a bad  approach, and you'll begin to understand why are other people recommending the other ways and design patterns, why do these languages and frameworks solve the problems the way they do etc. You can always refactor later, so don't be afraid if it doesn't turn out the best for the first few tries.

Languages are just tools. To me, there's no good or bad language in general. It always depends on the task you need to do. You have to pick the language and even framework that helps you the most to accomplish your goal for the right needs (system, performance, timeframe). Your choice is right if you don't feel that you're fighting against every tool constantly. And that's why you can't skip learning the language and practice coding in it. Without practice, you are never going to "level up".

If I also looked back the code I wrote as a novice in around  2007, I would also change several things to make the code more safe, testable, readable, and reusable.

author: @jasonvene
text: SyncMain's conclusion is spot on. I'd use the word practice. Practice writing, designing, debugging, diagnosing, re-writing, re-thinking. I started in C back in the 80's, moved to C++ in the very early 90's, and I'm currently making software in C++ 20. SyncMain's other message, opposing the C++ warnings from the public, is also spot on. If your targets require other languages then there's no reason to use C++ instead, but if your targets require C++ you shouldn't avoid it. It does require expertise, and that is one of the flaws of the language. Not everyone is suited to it. However, I can say from decades of experience, I have zero...zero...of the issues you read about "warning" about C++. I did have them, long, long ago, especially when I worked in C. My experience and training puts me in the position of automatically choosing better methods to write software, no matter what language I use. By far, C++ is my favorite and where I am most productive, but I have practiced long and hard. Consider, too, if you would really want to use software (if it is important software to you) that was built by someone without experience, expertise and serious knowledge. With that, the languages are less important than how they are used and what options those languages provide for solid, fast, efficient and reliable final products.

author: @puzzud
text:
My advice for newcomers:

Prioritize making (many) small functions.

Worry less about making efficient, proper, and even bugless code.

Make variable names meaningful--stay away from abbreviations.

Write comments as outlines for what you want to do; then as you implement them, remove each comment with a call to a well named function (usually some concise form of the comment). For me, comments are usually a sign that I need to extract a function or break up a function.

Following this advice should lay the foundation for code to be manageable and improvable.

author: @shahidullahmuffakir668
text:
Watch the video first and here is the summary:

Chris, who’s been working with C++ for about 15 years, talks about how he got started and what beginners should focus on. He even found one of his first C++ files from 2008, which made him reflect on how people today often overthink which language to learn.

His main point is simple: don’t stress too much about picking the “perfect” language. Just start coding. You’ll learn way more by actually writing code, breaking things, and fixing errors than by trying to follow the “right” path from the beginning.

He also mentions that beginners shouldn’t be afraid of writing bad or messy code. Looking back, he feels he would’ve improved faster if he had just experimented more instead of worrying about doing everything correctly.

Overall, his advice is to open your IDE and start building something — there’s no perfect way to begin, and nothing terrible will happen if you make mistakes.

author: @xealit
text: I would say, if your goal is more about the application side of things, changing files and putting something on screen etc, then indeed go with Python or Ruby or something else. Sure, you can do all of that in C++ and nowadays you do have excellent tools that make C/C++ palatable. VScode is there and is free. Even CMake gets better all the time. But, working with C++ means knowing how the computer works. It means knowing what is "compiling" and "linking". It means using gdb and knowing what are "symbols" and how actual memory works. On the other hand, how computer works is an exciting subject by itself. So, if you want to learn how the computer works, do not doubt trying C/C++. One thing to add, C/C++ are genetically the languages of all modern computing. So, it is definitely worth to know how that works. author: @distrologic2925
text:
C++ is the best way to start programming.

It is the largest ecosystem with the best compatibility, while being mostly low-level and true to the hardware.

Even if it is not the tool of choice for your task, it balances simplicity and expressive power well enough to learn the basics aswell as to venture into new territory and experiment.

With something like C you will get hung up with compiler settings and platform details and lack of convenience features.
With something like Java or Typescript you will miss out on most of the magic going on under the hood and will learn highly pragmatic and specialized styles of coding.

C++ seems right on the line between expressive power and runtime abstraction.

author: @Thugblader92
text:
My highschool teacher for 3 years of C++ programming kept teaching everything in bite sizes on purpose so I was absolutely never satisfied with my own code.
Write a simple world clock program? - week 1.
Write a word processor that accepts typewriting modules? - week 2.
Go back to the world clock, make it accept modules for timezones. - week 3.
Go back to the word processor, make it able to read and edit different file formats. - week 4.
Go back to the world clock, make it able to accept API from different online world clocks - week 5.
Project/test time: write a PDF editor that automatically puts timestamps with your world clock code in the word processor... - 3 weeks.

In essence, every time I went back to edit the previous work I got more and more disgusted with what I had written before, because I never did anything outside the scope of the assignment.
Now I can't write a single code without thinking "What if I want this and that at a later point", and take it into account... Has helped a lot, but my old projects look like garbage and your retrospective from looking at old code is very foreign to me. Thanks for sharing!

text: C++, done the right way (e.g. Auto Pointers, SafeInt...), can be a very good programming language. C is really problematic IMHO as you deal with void* all the time. I think whole preprocessor mayhem with #inlcude is now resolved. But still: you can go wrong really badly in C++ - but that is not unique to it. If you need very good performance and maximum portability C++ is absolutely worth considering. E.g. for gaming engines - maybe the only choice. For all the rest like GUI program, Web APIs / Sites, CLI - you are better of using the more modern languages. But: DO NOT fall into the rabbit holes of JS or Python. A STRONGELY typed language is MANDATORY for any serious, larger, long term maintenance project. Python is NOT typed at all. Neither is JS. TS is! Also: Python has terrible performance. So has JS. author: @Leo3ABPgamingTV
text:
I strongly disagree with the notion that C++ should not be a first programming language. When there is nothing to compare to, then all the "hard" and "scary" parts about C++ are just normal everyday stuff to you. And being an adept at C++ makes it so much easier to learn and understand many other programming languages. On the other hand, coming from other language like Python or C# one cannot help but see C++ through a prism of those languages and thus becoming frustrated from how "hard" C++ is (relative to those other languages).

On the other hand, I fully support that one should not get fixated on replicating the "only correct way to code" which too many beginner programmers seem to do. While there are code conventions and "ways" (Python vibes intensify), they are not the ultimate "be all - end all" laws of the universe and there is nothing wrong with developing your own coding style as long as it is consistent and works fine in an environment (i.e. company, or group of people) that you are working at.

author: @iofish__
text:
It depends what we're building. In the firmware or system-level space, Zig might take off and displace C, but it will be at least 15 or 20 years. C is deeply entrenched and it is loved religiously. What helps Zig is that it is totally interoperable with C and very much sticks to the C ethos while making really substantial improvements.

Mobile applications are pretty much going to stick to Java, Kotlin and Swift. There isn't any call for change in this area of industry I don't think.

In software more generally, it looks like there is a discontent with C++ because of the complexity of maintaining it. But porting large applications over to Rust is extremely costly. So, Rust is basically only getting used for new projects. It's just that existing projects are extremely mature and aren't going away anytime soon.

There's also areas that Rust just isn't likely to be apart of, like web backend. It's just really not necessary to use Rust when Go and Node exist. It just isn't specifically the right tool.

author: @steverempel8584
text:
C / C++ will never die because it's the original low level "High Level" language. 
It does something almost perfectly that nobody else is very interested in doing right now.  It is a high level language that is very close to machine level, so it runs efficiently and quickly.  It's old, so it is well known and there's no reason to replace it.
C++ will be just a little bit easier to replace than English at this point.
Any new language is more interested in compatibility with many environments, ease of programming, being a conceptually pure language, or doing something new. None of these goals work with making machine level code that runs quickly.

text:
well, cpp!? that's not even just one thing, and even then it has so many versions too 😂
What you actually meant to say is C is the language of the century, but there's no real c compiler anymore, it's all cpp.
The only thing we care abt is the ABI which largely is leaned on C.
So well if there's never gonna be a new interop, any language will eventually conform to the C ABI for the linkers, that's the whole reason we can use different languages together, bcs they all compile down to the same thing and can "just be linked" in the binary.

...but this guy thought Java would replace C?
A language dependent on a user installed lib + runtime 😂
What were you smoking!?

Anyhow, all these people fail to see progress on the horizon and can't think of anything outside their little bubble.
The next programming paradigm will be adjacent, it won't be a more high-level language like Java or Go, it won't be a more low level language either, like Rust or Zig, even tho compile time and meta programming like in jai or odin kinda go in the direction we need.
But they all fail to see the issue with todays programming, the paradigm.
Not what or where we code, but HOW.
How we code stayed largely the same, text, with no visual or logically connecting interface, it's just text, and you have to keep the entire mental overhead of control flow etc all in your head.
Compilers also are such different things nowadays than simply trying to transpile phrases into assembly...
One thing a compiler does, is first figuring out what you actually wanted to do, using markov chains, collapses them, unrolls loops, choose best instructions to solve a higher level logic problem.
All to say your compiler does so much work that is wasted and not iterated upon.
The act of coding, (no matter how much you color the text or link words so you can jump to definitions, and rename symbols etc is all just a crutch to hide the actual problem with programming.
Text.
Text has never been a good or even useful tool to describe complex logical processes and branches...
Especially when trying to be very precise and explicit, you now introduce the most wishy-washy syntax for it, which was english in the wisest decision ever made...

Which brings us to, how will we program in the future?
I for one, would like to imagine a world where you have instant retrospection and automatic reflection.
Logical dependencies are visually connected.
Control flow is literally a flow graph.
It's crazy to me, how many computations are easily representable as a graph on a whiteboard with little to no ambiguity, but then we try to code this up in words, just for the compiler to turn the code back into a graph 😂

author: @fyu1945
text:
Ugh this comment section is painful to read.

First of all, I can't imagine how someone in the 90s could seriously think Java would kill C++. Even if it hadn't run on a VM it still didn't have any low level access or abilty to minupulate simple non-OOP data except for some basic typse like ints and floats. And this wasn't 2025 with our new and shiny CPUs and GPUs. This was 90s, where there were still games being written in assembly. Java was just completely not for the job, C++ was doing.

And this is important, when we talk about "killing a language" in order for it to become obsolete, there has to be a language that can do everything C++ can and bring enough new things to the table, that it will be cost-effective to actually replace it.

Rust, unlike Java, actually can do everything a C++ can. On top of it, it's a modern language, without decades of backwards compatibility bs baggage that C++ inevitably acquired. It's memory-safe by default, thanks to the borrow checker, but let's remember, this is actually just RAII stolen from C++ itself. Only in Rust, it's in every library and program by default.

The only thing that Rust doesn't have is OOP, but that's on purpose, cause over the years the industry realized that it's not as good as we previously thought. Instead, Rust keeps the good part - interfaces (called traits) with dynamic dispatch done slightly differently than C++ with it's own benefits and draw backs.

And most importanly, if you do need to dabble in memory directly, you can use the unsafe keyword to dereference a raw pointer and have every single superpower C++ has. As a bonus, if you do end up with a memory bug, you know exactly were to grep for, unlke in C++ where a memory bug can appear anywhere.

So, Rust can do everything a C++ can. It can do it much more safely. There aren't 5 different ways to do the same thing, of which 3 were declared deprecated by the community 20 years ago. And on top of it, it brings years many of industry's developments, like Algebraic Data Types, Errors as values (which contrary to some commenters is good, because not only can exceptions get unhandled, resulting in a runtime error, but also many code bases can't afford the additional performance cost that exceptions bring) and many more.

With that, is this enough to kill C++? No.

First of all, when people talk about "killing C++" it doesn't mean that no one will use C++. Legacy code bases exist everywhere, and people still program in Cobol, Fortran and PHP. There's no way, any language, even a divine hypothetical perfect one could make C++ just disapear.

When talking about killing a language, what most mean is to make the Rust, in this case, a better alternative to C++ when starting a new project. This is much easier, but still incredibely difficult task, especially with C++.

Those who doubt Rust and say things like "It's been ten years and I still don't see it" forget just how monumental C++ ecosystem is. For decades it was the only low-level language that provided some higher level ergonomics. Hundreds of thousands of libraries were made with this language and NO. Rust is not going to replace it in a fucking decade. Expecting that is just being incredibely dishonest.

However, Rust is steadily getting larger. Today it's ready for production and many giants from sillicon valley are already implementing it. Linux is implementing it. Startups are implementing it. It's ready NOW. It has the most enthusiastic community out of any language and it's good. The only reason the Rust doubters are so vocal about it is that they heard about it and that's only, because Rust community is ready for this discussion, unlike other alternatives.

Of course, it's important to ask, should we even kill C++? Can't it just stay? I believe yes, we should. Not because I hate it, in fact I respect this language immensly. But it is unsafe. Even with the newest safety features, it doesn't really matter, cause the ecosystem is already set in stone. And it is old. We as developers and language creators learned a lot about designing programming languages. One only has compare Kotlin code with Java code to see this. We know what works and what doesn't. And unfortunately C++ has a lot of bad things in it, that were piled up over the years. No ammount of versions will fix that. So perhaps, it's time to let it rest for legacy code and start writing with a language that's cleaner and safer. That's of course just my opinion.

nobody ever expected java to kill c++!
Java will never fully replace C++ because it operates at a higher level of abstraction, relying on the Java Virtual Machine, which isolates it from direct hardware access and low-level system control. In contrast, C++ allows developers to manage memory manually, interact directly with hardware, and build critical components like operating system kernels, device drivers, and high-performance engines such as Unreal Engine. These capabilities require deterministic performance and fine-grained control that Java, with its garbage collection and runtime overhead, cannot consistently provide, making C++ indispensable for systems programming and performance-critical applications.
And this is why nobody ever expected java to kill c++!

author: @dr_jaymz
text:
I think the issue has always been squarely down to the way they are used in c.  You cannot intuitively infer what a * or & means if they used terms like addressof instead people wouldn't get so confused.  But its like that because only a few ascii symbols were available at the time and so that is the way that it is.  If you start by programming a simple micro controller using assembly its gets hard quickly, you basically need a higher level language to take care of branching and addressing memory - when you come at it from that angle it makes 100% sense to the point where you almost invent the need yourself - only to find c has your back. 
If you don't use c at least monthly you forget the syntax and thats when we get into the stabbing * or & in because we know its one of them of some form.
Efficient code uses pointers because its much faster to point  or reference  data than to keep moving it.  The downside is that since an address is just a number you can very easily point to memory that isn't what you intended.  Even the best programmers can easily get caught by an edge case - so there's a trade off between efficient and safe code - i.e. you can spend 20 instructions checking the bounds and 1 instruction copying data to be safe but thats inefficient, so it depends on what your doing.
By far the largest confusion for students are strings, char arrays, pointers to, const char arrays and when and which to use - discussion for another day.

The requirement for declaring variable types is often thought of as a limitation of C but, it's by design. To grasp that topic it is really helpful to generally know how  the (at least abstracted) hardware of a computer works. I've been lucky enough that I've been raised in the 80s, so I learned on computers where you needed to know how it works internally to program them. That creates a visual idea of what variables and pointers are.  
In C and C++ it can be even harder because you can even calculate with pointers. In other languages they exist for the same purposes explained in this (excellent) video but you can not calculate with them (Go e.g.). And languages like Java do have them only under the hood and you sometimes get an idea they exist internally when you hit something like a "NullPointerException".

author: @prabinlamsal74
text:
When you pass by value to a function: 
The changes done to the variables inside the function doesn't affect the real variable (unless we accept it back). 

When you pass by reference to a function: 
Since the parameter refers to the same variable being passed, any changes made inside the function will affect the real variable as well 

In modern languages like js, normal variables are passed by value and arrays etc are passed by reference. This is why we can edit the array in a function and the changes can be seen on the real array.

author: @ako-d2m
text:
In the C language spec declaration is in this format: [type] [declarators list] where [declarators list] is a list of declarators. Valid declarators include are [identifier], ([declarator]), *[declarator], [declarator](), or [declarator][[constant expression]]. That is to say - the * is part of the declarator, NOT part of the type - BUT neither is it part of the identifier. Here's the important note: functions are also declared using declarators; using the format [[declarator]([parameter list]). That is to say; "int a()" is a valid function or variable declaration. A declarator means "when you see this construct, it will give the specified type".

So what's the confusion with *? Some people incorrectly attach it to the type. From a language perspective it is part of the declarator, not the type. This will cause issues in a few cases;
int (*foo)(); <- impossible to understand this if you have the mindset * is part of the type!
int* a, b; <- in this example a is a pointer, but b is an int!

Take your time to understand what "int *a" actually means; it means if you deference a you get an integer. "Customer *user" means if you dereference user you get a Customer. It does not mean the type of user is a pointer to Customer. 

Eg:
int a = 0; // a is an integer with value 0
int *pa = &a; // dereferencing pa yields an int, point it to the address of a
*pa = 1; // dereference pa (follow the address back to a) and set the value to 1

See the pattern? "*pa" = "dereference pa". Now you can see how simple it really is. Eg; int *(*(*pa)(int))[10]; = dereferencing pa yields a function that takes an int as an argument that returns a pointer to an array of 10 pointers to ints. int *(*pa())() = pa can be dereferenced to yield a function that takes no args and returns a pointer to a function that returns an int.

author: @Muttisuri
text:
To be completely honest, I think I only started understanding pointers after playing with rust.
And I think I got it because the rust stuff is cleaver, they don't call it a pointer they use the word “reference” and somehow I think that made it easier for me. For usage, the fact that the pointer is “just a number” only makes it more confusing at the first approach (I know it's useful for incrementing, but that to me at the beginning is confusing questions).
And since &x is a “reference” to x I can then think of it at a more conceptual level. That added with the whole borrow checker thing of only one mutable reference allowed me to think in “references” not values without worrying about the technical details of hex numbers. Since I've seen people trying to learn C without having seen hex numbers before.

On the “incrementing issue” for me, it always caused some confusion due to the “assumption” that things can certainly be found by incrementing the pointer. I know that's true for arrays since they are defined by being contiguous in memory, but at the beginning you will likely think of them closer to lists.
Paradoxically, I think the more “complicated” and abstract language is better to teach. So you are first thinking of the logic of the program, and when you get that you can use it to anchor your newly acquired knowledge of the computer's internals.

EDIT: Also the usage of “reference” makes the term dereference be clearer, at least to me.


TL;DR I think we should stop using the word pointers and use the more descriptive word “reference”

author: @pjl22222
text:
Variables on the stack is not static memory. Static memory is for variables that are either global variables declared outside any function or variables inside functions declared as static (like "static int x"). Those aren't allocated on the stack but in a different memory area set aside for all the static and global variables. Technically there are two areas for static/global variables, the data segment for initialized variables and the bss segment (which is filled with zeros) for uninitialized ones. They are located towards the bottom of the memory map just above the text segment which contains all the code and is the lowest segment.

Variables on the stack are called automatic variables and there is actually a keyword "auto" you can use to declare them but auto is the default so "int x" actually means "auto int x" in contrast to "static int x" but you'll never see auto in any actual code.

author: @matthewbutner8696
text:
I've explained pointers the exact way you have to my class for years and it still is a great struggle for them. Mainly when it pointers that require more than one level of indirection (int**, int***) etc. This confusion tends to compound here because pointers can be both used to indicate (multi-dimensional) arrays or that we want to modify the value whose address we are being passed. So if your function gets an int*** is it a 3D array or the address of a 2D array that we want to modify? The answer comes down to the context but my students don't have sufficient experience to be able to fully grasp the context yet. 

One idea that I'm going to try this quarter is to help reinforce the code to English idea as well as try and remove some of the confusing pointer syntax is to make some simple macros
# define addressOf(x) &x
# define valueAt(x) *x

hide the macros from the students, and then introduce these pointer concepts by using "the built-in functions addressOf and valueAt" at first before I reveal to them the ugly truth. Here's hoping it helps some. I also try and pass this video along to them in case hearing the same thing but in a different voice helps.

text:
For anyone who's still confused.

A pointer is a variable that contains a memory address of a variable. 
To access a variable's memory address, you use "&" operator.

For example, if i have a variable called "a" that contains an integer. "&a" would return the memory address of variable "a"

To access the value of a memory address, you use a "*" operator. So, if i have a pointer called "px" that contains the memory address of variable "x":

x = 20;
px = &x;

To access the value, of memory address of variable "x", you use this: *px.

author: @TheMrTape
text:
1:39 "I put the number 0x1000 at 0x1004. I've just created a pointer. A pointer is just a value that happens to be an address."

All this is false. A value that happens to be an address is definitely not a pointer; it requires your intent to use it as such, because pointers exist as an abstract idea in your head as a programmer, not as a distinct physical state on the die.

Therefore it only becomes a pointer when you intend it to, even if it's not used, and even if it's pointing to an invalid address, because it's not a pointer at all, it's just a number, and the rest is you arbitrarily pretending otherwise.

Using something in an abstract fashion, meaning you pretend a thing is something beyond its physical state, and calling it accordingly, is solely based on your intent and imagination.

Anything beyond the on/off state of individual bits, like numbers or even calling the on/off state 1/0, is abstraction to some degree. Most functionality isn't really there before you intend it to, either directly or on behalf of the compiler, unless it exists as a distinct purpose-built function on the die; even then we define its output abstractly and use it as such, but the underlying physical function wouldn't be an abstraction.

author: @telephrag
text:
Ok, I have couple gripes with this video.
1) Don't declare  "using namespace std;" globally. It can cause ambiguities. 
2) std::unique_ptr doesn't do what you say. Firstly, raw pointer is simply a variable that contains address to data of a certain type. int*, for example, points to date with type of int, char* to data with type of char, etc... std::unique_ptr is a wrapper over raw pointer that is deallocated on stack (at the end of {} block). When end of the {} block is reached destructor of class std::unique_ptr is being called which in turn calls destructor of an object the std::unique_ptr pointer was pointing at. When it comes to raw pointer only the variable that contains the address would be deallocated while data at said address would remain with no reference to access it (provided that data was created with "new" and assigned to pointer or created outside of this {} block).

Now think of ICopyable in C#. Now imagine that this property is explicitly deleted inside std::unique_ptr class. That means that the pointer can no longer be passed by copy into anything thus guaranteeing that one and only one reference to given piece of data exists. If you still want to pass it around you can use std::move but it will null the pointer at place where you passed it from.

Alternatively if you want to pass pointer to data around you can use std::shared_ptr which again is wrapper over raw pointer but it can be copied and atomically counts the amount of references to data across the program. Once the count reaches zero data is being deallocated.

author: @KenJackson_US
text:
I wrote C and then C++ for years as an embedded software developer.  As the language grew more and more complex, I noticed developers very purposely wrote more and more complex code which took longer and longer to read, trace and understand.

Worse, there was a convoluted arrogance that came along with it.  If you couldn't understand their extremely convoluted code, you were a lesser person.  Few acknowledged that convoluted code was bad code.

And discussions about the language replaced abstract discussions about what the compiler and processor would have to do to accomplish something.  It became essentially _wrongthink_ to even consider how a compiler would implement code.

While I was constantly striving to simplify the organization of data and the processing of it, my coworkers were constantly building empires of more and more complex code to their own glory.  They _hated_ me when it got in my way and I simplified it.

author: @shimadabr
text:
About C++ security, I think most of the common problems that Rust solved, C++  already did too. The "problem" is that while in Rust they're there by default (and you can't escape it), in C++ they're opt-in (but highly encouraged by the community) features or patterns like smart pointers, RAII, etc. Smart pointers are, in practice, C++ ownership system.

C++ has a legacy of 30+ years, so a lot of legacy code and "legacy programmers" still use the old verbose, unsafe patterns, it's also the style teached at most universities (remember folks, professors usually don't stay up to date with the industry or language features). But I see a lot of effort by the community to enforce these new patterns and document them. For beginners it's a challenge to soak up and distinguish so much legacy knowledge together with the new knowledge. But I'm having a lot of fun in my journey.

Professional C++ programmer here:
The thing is that C++ has a steep learning curve and that most developers just don't want to invest the time to learn the language. Just as you've said: with great power comes great responsibility and rarely anybody wants to be responsible because it is hard. Also C++ is usually taught wrong and rarely do teachers or courses explain that, for example, raw ( C ) pointers are not evil, they just cannot be owning pointers. 
I agree with your suggestion on how to learn C++, I would just add that after learning C, fammiliarize yourself with the abstractions that the language introduces, by reading books and watching convention lectures.
That way you get a bottom up ( learning C and the memory model) and top down (learning abstractions) view of the language.
You just need time to understand the language, something that most people do not have today.
C++ is not a perfect language, but it does not deserve the hate it gets.

author: @jeremygrice311
text:
Coming to this a year later to say that I disagree with the argument about "sugar". In the on-screen example, using iterators to step through a vector of numbers is obviously a silly way of just stepping through 0..3. But if you do have an iterable STL container that you want to iterate over, then you should use iterators. Comparing them to a for-loop that increments an integer doesn't do it justice.

Suppose you have a vector of 10 elements. You write a for loop that increments a value from 0 to 9 and uses that to index the vector and access each element. So far so good. But now imagine that your code-base has grown massively, and a shared pointer to that vector is passed to a function running on a different thread that changes the size of the vector. Now, your for-loop is either broken because the size of the vector has changed, or is slow because you rewrite it to check the value of the integer against the size of the vector with every iteration.

The clear solution here is an iterator. The loop will terminate when the iterator exceeds the memory owned by the vector, but no member functions need to be called to get a size value for comparison. By using iterators from the start, and always using them, your codebase is safe, consistent, easier to read (because you don't have two types of loops doing the same thing with STL containers) AND futureproofed. It's not sugar, it's an efficient high-level abstraction that will keep your program memory safe.

Also, the template "example" at 2:05 isn't unreadable because it makes use of templates, it's unreadable because of the way it has been formatted and the lack of descriptive variable names. You could write C code that looks just as bad.

Honestly this whole video feels like a bunch of unfair examples crafted to make C++ look worse than it is. Some examples of the features you're critical of in use-cases where they make sense would be much better. For example, implementing a container like a linked list in C requires that you either rewrite it by hand for every type you want to have lists of (which is all templates actually do anyway), or write a generic implementation that uses void pointers, discarding valuable type information. Templates allow you to implement once, and compile to a whatever type targets you need. Best of both worlds.

author: @ThisIsLiam-m6j
text:
- C++ introduced smart pointers in C++11 to move people away from raw pointers; the main source of issues in C.
- The idea that beginners should learn C before C++ is completely wrong. Teaching C first leads students to carry over C-style practices that C++ was designed to avoid and abstract away.
- Linus Torvalds' criticism of C++ is a major talking point for Zig and Rust developers. It's surprising how much he dislikes C++, even though many Linux developers would love to switch; just like Windows, macOS, and Android already have.
- The famous quote, "C makes it easy to shoot yourself in the foot. C++ makes it harder, but when you do, it blows your whole leg off," is often misinterpreted. Bjarne Stroustrup meant that C++ avoids C’s common pitfalls but introduces rarer, harder-to-debug issues; not that C++ is worse than C.
- "Avoid sugar"? Comparing a loop using iterators with a vector vs. a simple for-loop with i is pointless; they serve different purposes.

author: @gamerk316
text:
Taking the char * example given in this video, I do agree it's use is frowned upon except in the specific case of cross-platform messaging (where you want to guarantee no compiler dependent behavior/sizing, which even std::string doesn't provide across platforms/compilers); use of std::string is *much* preferred in all cases because it's a proper object, with all the features and protections that come along with it.

The issues I come across with C++ are typically one of the following:

1: The fact the feature set is so robust turns people off, because there's multiple ways to accomplish the same task.  Example: Iterating over the range of an object; the *old* way would be a FOR loop using the start/end values and in iterator, but you now have ranged-based FOR loops (as of C++11) that do the same thing in an easier syntax.

2: Thinking of C++ as "C with Classes" and not taking advantage of the fact C++ is (mostly) an object-oriented language.

3: Trying to use C++ in a role another language can do better.  Need a simple GUI o n Windows?  Use C# (even I hate C++ Message Maps).  Simple console app?  Just use C.  And so on.

author: @metal571
text:
Learning C first will tend to lead a developer towards a C-like C++ style. This tends to defeat the purpose of C++; See Kate Gregory's talk "Stop Teaching C".

Avoiding sugar is also not the best approach, and in fact the range for loop over a std::vector generates less assembly instructions than using a traditional loop variable. You can prove this in Compiler Explorer with -O3 and is mentioned in Bjarne's book A Tour of C++ 3rd Edition. This makes some sugar in C++ what Jason Turner calls a "negative cost abstraction".

Also "near zero cost" is not quite right. The language design involves what they call the Zero Overhead Principle, which is often misunderstood. This means not that there is actually zero overhead in using an abstraction, but that if you implemented it manually by hand using only C or assembly, you wouldn't be able to do better. At least, that's the goal...I won't go into how exceptions allocating and Run Time Type Identification are clearly in violation of this.

author: @FuzzhyFoo
text:
I don't think people have to learn C first. As a starting language, I think C++ contains a much simpler language trying to break free, chained down by legacy. I feel we scare away people from it by spooking them with scary concepts like pointers, references and memory safety. As though that is something exclusive to C/C++.

If I were to introduce someone to programming through C++, I wouldn't teach them about raw memory allocation. No pointers, pointers to pointers, or even references. Reduce the friction between them and their code until it becomes relevant to understand the more core concepts. Let them pass variables by copy while they're learning. Move semantics have reduced the overhead of that dramatically. Let them return copies, they don't have to understand copy elision or NRVO. You don't teach someone java or C# by telling them how to appease the garbage collector. 

It's naive, yes. But even basic things in C can appear arcane. Take the supposedly safe "sprintf" - lovely name. 
You need to understand stack vs heap allocation, when to alloc/free. null terminators, the caveats of the sprintf family of functions, the 'safe' versions of them, what that strange 'restrict' keyword means, etc. 

Of course, there are nice, basic, declarative examples like adding strings together, which while basic, lets beginners appreciate how that happens under the hood.

author: @the-programing
text:
From doing a personal projects (around 100,000 lines+ of code) using C++, C, Java, TypeScript/Javascript, and ObjectiveC, I truly think c++, Java, or ObjectiveC are the best languages simply because they all offer near zero cost for abstractions. For example, when I was writing TS in ReactNative I wrote a lot of classes and abstractions, but the performance gets worse and worse to the point a cold start takes more than 10 seconds, which I just recently found out TS doesn’t “compile” to js but simply translates to js. I was expecting TS can “unroll” the classes to js. This causes the project to get extremely bloated since you have to write as much logic into the same file as possible to preserve performance. I am not very experienced with javascript, but this property alone makes me dread writing any js.

In C++, you can write pure C style, zero class projects; or, you can write completely object oriented project. Both styles will give you the same performance (some times the oop style will give you a better performance due to the -O2 level optimization the compiler can re-reference the class structures to decrease binary size, but C style code doesn’t have that information). I personally think oop offers clearer abstractions while writing code, and in the long run make the project scale a lot easier. That’s why I personally prefer it. 

However, I think anyone who can proficiently write C style code should NOT switch to C++. If you can write scalable C code, C++ definitely offers little value for you. Even so, I recommend anyone who is starting programming to start with C++ or Java, because these languages helps you to learn about structuring a project that can be scaled from the start. And you can switch to C style languages at a later date without any trouble.

author: @Spiderboydk
text:
I switched from C++ to C a few years ago and never regretted it.

The main reason is C++ is so endlessly complex that takes a big cognitive toll in your head while developing.

There is no such thing as not paying for features you don't use, because even if you don't use them, you still have to know about them and deal with them. You can't just ignore knowing about exceptions, move semantics, overload resolution, etc.

C++ also likes to hide a lot of code from you in constructors, destructors, operator overloads, etc. so seemingly innocent statements like x = y + z; might execute all sorts of code from all over the code base. You really have to have a good knowledge of the code base to understand what's going on. It makes it hard to ballpark how fast or slow code might be.

Switching to C freed up a lot of mental capacity I can now spend on actual problem solving.

text: There are several features of C++ that I like, however, it can also be greatly abused.  I use C or C++ depending on the application being implemented.  I like C++ function overloading when implementing applications that will grow over time.  But for embedded systems, C is more straight forward, has a smaller footprint, and is better for programming down the the bare metal.  For web apps, accounting apps, etc, C++ is a better fit.  Choosing C vs C++ is also depending on if you're writing your own apps completely standalone, or, if you will be interfacing to 3rd party libraries.  Sometimes you don't have luxury to choose, depending the environment you're working in.  Unless you are the boss, you may be required to work in C, C++, Python, etc, etc.   If you're looking for work or a career in some field, the more languages you learn, the more job possibilities there will be.

My opinion on c++:
c++ has it's advantages, but it introduces a bunch of headaches if you don't know every little detail, and it has a lot of stuff to it, so it can be overwhelming to learn, but if you have the patience/time to learn it all, I would rather suggest you try rust instead, because that way you avoid the memory management headaches you get with c++, and the compiler helps you avoid a lot of mistakes. Additionally, since C++ is as old as it is, there is a lot of legacy code that people rely on, which means they can't suddenly change something that breaks that legacy code, which means that all future updates will just add a bunch of unnecessary bloat that makes it even harder to fully learn.
tl;dr: C++ has had some yeas of glory, but it is time to move on to newer and better languages, like Rust, and eventually Jai.

author: @sw33t.angela
text:
So, the reason for not wanting to use raw strings in C++ is due to raw C strings being actually unsafe. Null termination relies on the string having it, and, if it's missing, some copy mechanisms break due to buffer overflow. These are why there are so many strcpy functions because the checks that you get what you expect and never overflow is needed. It also relies on single byte ASCII characters and can't accommodate multibyte UTF-8 charsets.

Std::string and by proxy Rust strings include the string length in bytes inside the structure so it can be safely dealt with without relying on external functions and dealing with memory management directly.

Not to say that c strings are all bad. If you have a stream of characters that there's no expected length and needs an end character, then null terminated strings are good.

author: @shimadabr
text:
Just a little correction, structs and classes in C++ are basically the same thing, except in classes it's possible to define the usual qualifiers for its members (private, protected, public...). That means you can define functions, constructors and destructors on structs as well (unlike C), but since all members are public, it's recommended to be used when dealing with a "pure data" object.
Also, one interesting fact that surprised me: Classes in C++ can be instanced at the stack, you don't need to use "new" or create/allocate a smart pointer.

Edit: As pointed out below, actually it's possible for structures to have access modifiers. The only difference then between both is the default access modifier (private for classes and public for structs).

author: @rockpadstudios
text: For low level embedded programming, C++ is overkill.  In the last 20 years I've come into many failing projects and the reason is C++ bloat.  With limited memory, C++ just bloats the code even when you use C+ and turn off RTTI, virtual classes, and exceptions.  I recently had to redo a product and the old one was all C++, factory patterns, singletons, etc. and it was nearly impossible to figure out where the code was at any instant in time.  With message queues and pointer passing, even when you hit a breakpoint you only get a pointer or function pointer and it's really hard to find out where the message came from since the messages typically don't have a sender in the object.  In embedded systems you will typically only have one of every major object (screen, keypad, etc.) so you don't really need classes.  I create a base class struct so each object can have a common interface and register an error callback etc. and it works great.  It would be nice if C pointers to functions could have more type checking but pointers to functions is all you really need.  I love C++ but C++11 and C++14 is a whole new language and most companies don't need that power.  Most use Java/C# for GUI's anyway now.  C++ is still the best for server based backend code that need efficient code execution when grid power is the limiting factor.  Spinning up C# or Java apps is not cost effective.  I recently worked with a C++ SDK for a BLE SOC from Microchip that was C++ and what a nightmare (so glad we didn't pick that chip).  Like all designs there was a "god class" with hundreds of small classes in it so the call tree just to blink an LED was 5 calls deep.  What a mess and the RTOS was non-standard and hard to compile out.

I agree that it shouldn't be your first language, but I don't agree that you should learn C first.  You should treat C and C++ as completely different languages.

Most people don't write C++ like C.  Programs in each language are architected and organized completely differently.  Approaching the language like it's C with extra features means that you're not taking advantage of what C++ offers you.  Most real world C++ codebases look a lot more like Java with the stick removed from its ass.

There's exceptions, of course - Arduino being one of them.  If you're in a resource-constrained environment then there's an argument for making your C++ look like C.  If you're working on larger microcontrollers or doing application programming, C will only hold you back.

author: @XiremaXesirin
text:
I think it's worth talking about why, precisely, C++ programmers don't like certain C-style conventions.

To use malloc/pointers as an example, the main reason we don't like malloc is because on its own, it doesn't express ownership―a concept that is really important to memory management and preventing memory leaks, but which isn't enforced by the language at all in C, or is automagically managed in garbage-collected languages like Java or python. When you write something like int* value_ptr = malloc(4); in C, there's no enforcement at the language level that the memory you allocated will later be cleaned up. The only way to ensure that is for the programmer to be a good girl and remember to clean it up.

But in C++, we express the same concept as auto value_ptr = std::make_unique<int>(); which does nearly the same thing as the C code (it also initializes the memory to a default value, which the C code doesn't do; this can be good or bad depending on whether you actually needed the memory initialized) but also has the extremely valuable benefit of preventing memory leaks. The programmer doesn't have to remember to write value_ptr.reset() at the end of its use; the language automatically calls the destructor when value_ptr falls out of scope, freeing the memory at the exact moment it is no longer being used.

Of course, there are occasionally situations where malloc and manual memory management (or memory management by an external library) are what you need, and C++ offers that stuff for compatibility, which makes the language more complex (and potentially dangerous), but also more flexible.

There's other examples I could cite which have their own debates (C-style unions vs std::variant, C-style arrays vs std::vector or std::array) but a lot of the same points apply to those cases.

author: @rnz2363
text:
There is one thing that you forgot.

Why the hell would we learn C++ when we can learn Rust ?

Linus Torvalds refused to use C++ instead of C, but agreed to use Rust for the Linux kernel. 

It means everything.

C++ is indeed inferior to Rust : 

- It is more complicated
- It is less readable, syntax can go terrible
- It is very not safe to use. at least half of all security vulnerabilities are due to these old languages
- It does not force you to handle errors, C++ programs cannot be as robust as Rust
- C++ exceptions are so bad
- It is not easy to use, no provided dependency management system, no provided linter/formatter. CMake is garbage and no one likes it. Visual Studio is so terrible i don't even want to say a word about it.
- The STL is clusterfucked because of interoperability with C types
-  Even modern C++ does not look modern when compared to Rust
- It is a pain to make portable code or real apps
- No official package registry, you either write everything or use gigantic libraries.
- Multithreading is just scary to use

It only takes a few weeks to learn Rust and it's just a relief : 

- Just as fast as C/C++
- Memory safe and you don't even have to deal with allocation by yourself, safe multithreading is also enforced by the compiler.
- Official package registry and dependency management system
- Suitable for anything, even embedded devices
- Very nice standard library.
- FFI with other languages such as C, because we still live in a C world
- Modern syntax and features, just as powerful as C++, but so much simpler (generics, traits, macros...).
- Easy to use, test, benchmark and everything, it's all included in the box
- Does not even have the concept of a null pointer.
- If you really want to do whatever you want (like using C-like pointers), you can also use unsafe Rust. But you are never actually required to do it in most cases.
- No garbage collector, no reference-counting pointers unless you ask for it.
- Will never have any breaking change for the language itself
- Huge community and almost 100.000 packages already available
- Ready for the web and even for frontend programming, using webasm

The only caveat is that Rust is pretty slow to compile, but maybe it will improve in the future.

Everything in Rust beats C++. 

There can be no denial about that. 

It is just a matter of time before Rust replaces C++.
