author: @maelstrom57
text:
Will you do one of these for JavaScript? Here are some ideas off the top of my head:

- End each line with a semicolon. VSCode has an option to insert semicolons automatically on file save.
- Ditch == and !=. If you want to compare a string and a number, cast one to the type of the other and compare them with === or !==.
- Declare your variables with `const` and `let`. Ditch `var`.
- Use `const` rather than `let` if you're never going to reassign the variable.
- Prefer template literals over string concatenation.
- Don't define all your functions in one file; use modules.
- Don't pollute the global scope. Prefer local variables.
- Avoid if-else hell; use switches when you can.
- Avoid if-else hell; use early returns.
- Avoid callback hell; use async/await.
- Simple callbacks should be written as arrow functions. `array.every(num => num % 2 === 0)` reads better than `array.every(function(num) { return num % 2 === 0; })`. I'd argue it's better to write all callbacks as arrow functions but that's just my opinion.
- Destructure arrays and objects when needed. Write `const { username } = req.body;` rather than `const username = req.body.username;`.
- When a function has many parameters, replace them with a destructured object so you can pass in arguments in any order.
- Prefer for...of-loops over traditional for-loops. Write `for (const item of array)` rather than `for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++)`, especially if you don't need i.
- Document your code either with JSDoc for vanilla JS or explicit types for TypeScript.
- Avoid the `argument` keyword in favor of rest parameters.
- Instead of filtering an array and then mapping it, which involves iterating over it twice, use `reduce` to do it all in a single iteration.
- The `includes` method is there to tell you if an array contains a given element or if a string contains a given substring. Stop writing `array.indexOf(value) > -1` like they did in the old days.
- Don't add methods to the built-in constructors. This could break your code in the future. Define classes that extend them instead.
- Don't use HTML attributes for event listeners, that's an old Internet Explorer practice we don't need to follow anymore. Have all your event listeners in your JS file and add them to your elements using the `addEventListener` method.

author: @ABaumstumpf
text:
for "std::endl" i would say it is the exact opposite.
Printing like this is done usually for one of 2 reasons:
1 - user interactions. You tell the user what is going on and ask him for an input
2 - tracing - you wanna see what the program did.
In the first case the performance is a complete non-issue, in the second case NOT using "std::endl" would be moronic cause in the case of an error you have no idea when it happend as you did not flush the buffer, not even considering yet that your claim about it taking extra time is actually not really that correct.
Often saw people try to be "clever" and avoid the supposed performance-impact of flushing that later get frustrated cause they can not find out what went wrong cause their logging is not showing them what is really going on.

People think/claim this makes such a large difference yet don't even know that 'sync_with_stdio' is a thing - by default the I/O-buffer used by std::cout is synchronised  with the buffer of the old c-streams. This alone has far bigger of an impact than std::endl vs \n. If flushign the buffer makes ANY relevant performance difference then you are well beyond newbie-territory and at that point you really should know a lot more about the standard behaviour of streams and their buffers.


Structured binding - that is still relatively knew and very often simply not available. Nearly no business-software created before 2018 will even use C++17, often still c++11. Upgrading your entire platform on an existing codebase is rather laborious.
Right now i am glad that we can use C++17 in most of our current projects, but in some i am still restricted to 14 or 11, really looking forward to C++20 with the easier string-formatting.

Awesome video. I know some people with years and years of experience who keep doing some of these. Especially returning by parameter and move-return. I've seen a code base where literally every function had a 'return std::move'.

'constexpr' in the case you showed would most probably not do anything as long as you have a good compiler and some level of optimization enabled. 'constexpr' / 'consteval' is more useful when you have to use the result of the function in a template parameter or another compile time thing.

The magic numbers one is true for virtually every language XD Still technically counts, though, so good one.

The cases where you pass a pointer into the function could be a reference instead, so there's no need to worry about ownership or null. If you want to be able to pass a null to mean nothing, then use std::optional. I can't think of a reason to use raw pointer, except for interop with C.

author: @TheEragonFreak
text:
nice video and very helpful. if you ever plan to extend this list in another video, i have a few requests to be covered:

- casting types with (type)variable when static_cast<type>(variable) should be used
- using if's when static_assert are more suitable
- not using the rule of five
- using typedef instead of using
- not using ADL 
- not using and not understanding the difference between constexpr, friend constexpr and inline constexpr
- relying on C macros when constexpr could be used
- assuming certain practices make your program run fast, but not benchmarking your code (this is less specific to c++ but there are many things where c++ beginners lean towards premature optimization, e.g. due to thinking raw pointers make a difference vs std::vector, when one can only be certain if it's been benchmarked)
- thinking assembly code is correlated to speed of program, while only benchmarks can give certainty
- thinking const unique_ptr<type>& is the same as const type*
- since many c++20 features are commonly supported nowadays, one could also talk about these, e.g. std::span, or std::format, but that could also be a separate video

in general, what i see among scientists who write code for computational stuff is that many scientists first learn C, then c++ where they are told it's just an extension of C. Thus they write C style code with a few c++ supplements, not thinking or not knowing about how different the languages are.

author: @sheeftz
text:
1. Using std::string, using std::cout ect. has the same drawback as using namespace std. You are make a choice for someone that 'string' will refer to 'std::string' and cout will refer to std::cout. You are substituting one evil with another, instead of solving it.
If it's domestic code, don't be afraid of using namespace std. If you'll use 'using std::something;' instead, you'll end up using all of the most populare std names in your headers anyway, and all your header files will begin with a screen of text telling "using std::this; using std::that; using std::those_two; using std::half_of_the_rest_library". This is not what you want.
If it's a public library code than use a library namespace, otherwise you are doomed to use std qualifier before every single std name.
3. Don't use 'auto' keyword without a purpose. The 'auto' keyword was designed to solve certain kind of problems. The given example is not in the list. Using 'auto' without a purpose makes your code hard to read. Use auto in general code (templates) or when type referencing is tedious (i.e. typename std::unordered_map<std::string, std:int32_t>::const_iterator).
5. There is nothing wrong in using C arrays. Using a core part of a language can not be wrong. There is std::span to solve the problem with function parameters.
6. Regarding the famouse Quake 3 code. Note that C style casting converts one type of pointer to another type of pointer. This is not UB. UB is dereferencing it because it violates type aliasing rules.
12. If you want to return multiple parameters, use std::tuple instead. It helps to avoid unnecessary struct declaration.

Overall good tips.

text: Great video! I have a couple critiques. #10: Even if the string literal outlives its scope, I wouldn't generally recommend writing an interface that implies returning a pointer to a local. As a consumer of this function, its interface alone is enough to make me at least suspicious about whether it invokes undefined behavior. Coupled with your points on RAII, I might also wonder who owns the character array, given that this function is returning a raw ("non-owning") pointer. If you find yourself writing a function that returns a constant expression, just define the constant expression directly---their lifetimes are not dependent on some blackbox implementation, and the ownership is clearly global and not my problem. #12: You don't need to define a dedicated structure type just to group some data. This is exactly what std::pair and std::tuple are for. As #11 discusses, they can also be used with structured bindings. If you want it to have a nicer name, use a typedef.

text: Casting away const is sometimes correct.  In controllers, the overwhelming design requirement is efficiency during a synchronized handler routine.  That handler routine may run for months or years.  The handler is critical, and owns its system.  No indirection cost is justified in such a handler.  Handlers require complex, interdependent tables, mappings, filters all built at startup, in multiple, phased, i/o based calculations.    At runtime, handler data flows, but configuration should be const.  The const-ness of elaborate, interdependent startup data must occasionally be defeated to complete a multi-pass initialization.

author: @LarryRuane
text:
Thank you, great video! Especially enlightening for me was the description of structured bindings; I see `first` and `second` used all over the place in bitcoin core. I knew item 30 (const ptr versus ptr to const) from many years of C programming; the mental model I used is: if the `const` is to the left of the `*`, then the thing pointed to is const; if it's to the right, then the pointer itself is const. And it can make sense to have both! `const S * const p` means that what p points to can't change, nor can p itself. Or even `const S * const * const p` (p is a pointer to a pointer to S; none of these 3 things can change). 

Another thing people often don't realize is: don't write `int * const p` in a declaration (header file), just write `int *p`, even if the function definition (implementation) is `int * const p`. This is because p being immutable is an implementation detail of the function, not part of its interface.

author: @zvxcvxcz
text: People say that about using endl;... and yeah, it is much slower because it flushed the buffer.  But you can't just say that without the corresponding warning.  They're going to get a segfault sooner or later and try to find it quickly with some debug lines... and since they passed the output line without flushing the buffer the segfault can occur before the buffer flush and they won't actually know if that line was reached or not that way.  So personally... I tend to print my errors always with endl; and file output lines with \n.  Logging might be a tough choice, there are libraries that handle it, but if doing one's own... on the one hand you want to log everything, and on other hand you want it all logged with minimal performance overhead.  You can do it, but it is beyond the total noob, need proper error handling that will flush the buffer still after the error.

text: So not to kneckbeard too hard, but I would disagree with "never use new / delete" slightly. Imagine you want some object to live across the application lifespan (like a static or global variable). author: @petrocksgarage
text:
#12 (out-params instead of returning a struct) at 4:47, setting up a one-off struct is a n00by move, IMO.  Return a pair or tuple and the caller can still use structured bindings.
#14 (forgetting to mark destructor virtual) at 5:21, there is a compiler warning for that: GCC_WARN_NON_VIRTUAL_DESTRUCTOR that works in both gcc & clang. I don't know about other compilers.
#15 (thinking class members init in order of init list) at 6:10, there is a warn for this too. -Wreorder-ctor
#18 (modifying a container while looping over it) at 7:41, Debug STL (-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG compiler flag) will catch this at runtime.  Its best to only enable Debug STL in debug builds because it can hurt perf.

I'd also add 3 more:
- using shared_ptr when a unique_ptr would express the ownership & memory lifetime better. e.g. as a stack or class member variable.
- Not obeying the Rule of Three/Five/Zero.
- Implementing a simple copy/move/default constructor or copy/move operator=(...) when '= default' would do the trick.

Other than that, I agree with you completely.

author: @FalcoGer
text:
5:15 that is not correct. constexpr is often misunderstood. it doesn't mean it can be calculated at compile time. In fact, it has nothing to do with optimization at all. Computing values like that at compile time has been a thing for decades and is optimization 101. what constexpr actually means is that the value can be used in a compile time context, such as assigning it to a constexpr or constinit variable, or using it as a template argument, etc.
to add to 12:19. make_unique handles exceptions in the constructor of whatever you are creating. And make_shared makes sure it allocates the control block (the thing that holds the refference count) along with your object in one allocation, which is much more efficient.

I'm late to the party, but I want to point out that raw pointer *are* bad especially how you showed them. Lvalue reference are a kinda non-owning pointers, *not* raw pointer.

On top of being explicitely non owning, they can be a simpke alias to the value being pointed to *if* a pointer is not needed, and under some circumstances might be ellided by compilers, if taking a pointer is useless (e.g. int const & could be transformed copying the int, or leaving it in the register, since sizeof(int) <= sizeof(int *) on modern architecture).

Raw pointer are a useful tool, but what you showed wasn't a correct use of them.
Also "raw pointer are non owning by convention" depends a lot of which convention you're speaking of, and is not a standard thing afaik

text: there's always this misunderstanding that "undefined behavior" means "anything can happen" but that's not really what it means. it just means that the standard itself provides no implementation details for the behavior. you can still know what WILL happen under certain circumstances. where it becomes a problem is past a certain point, your code's complexity gets to a degree that you _probably wont_ know what will happen if you use a lot of undefined behavior, or if the behavior may change from OS to platform to implementation (and whatever-else weird in-betweens you have based on how you are compiling) which is usually why undefined behavior exists. in some cases, undefined behavior doesnt change in those situations and are undefined behaviors for reasons that dont affect you at all. sometimes, things really are just undefined behavior because the _standard_ doesnt provide implementation details and that's it, but that the way it is implemented is still done the same way practically everywhere (such as casting ints to chars in C). another reason why undefined behavior exists is because there is a problem that has multiple solutions that are all valid.

For 25, there is one case where you would want to use new instead of unique ptr. When you have a long lived singleton type object, you can run into static destructor cataclysms where an object is destroyed but it was depended on by a separate static object. Static destructor memory issues are horrible to debug as there's no usable stack, just _exit.
Now, the concept of a singleton is quite nasty but when you truly have global state like a logger or multithreaded exception handler it's not super great to pass it 12 layers deep into your implementations... So keeping in mind that for certain cases, when leaky singletons are required... New has its use. Bonus: Valgrind and address sanitizer fully support this pattern and won't flag the leak.

author: @1b2m
text:
Good video. But for someone who's so strict about wrong and right ways of coding, I noticed one of the most newbie mistakes in your on-screen code. And that is the placement of the * and & symbols when declaring, assigning or otherwise using pointers and references and addresses.

When you declare a variable "int number = 5;" then "number" is a label for a memory container. At declaration time, the compiler takes note of where in memory the container is, and (by being declared as int) how many bytes of coherent memory it has assigned, and also how these bytes should be interpreted. (Think signed/unsigned bit use, or float/double splitting of sign/exponent/fraction bits.)

So when you use it in your code as e.g. "std::cout << number;" then the compiler sees your use of the label "number", goes looking where in memory it points to, how many bytes of memory to read from there, and in what way it should interpret the bits/bytes there. In the end, it will substitute the label "number" with the collected and converted int representation of what was stored in the memory container.

This means that the label "number" is, effectively - in code, equivalent to an integer with the bits arranged to represent the value 5. So the data type of the label "number" is an integer. As simple as that.

Now, when you take the address of that integer variable, e.g. like "&number", then the & is in a way a modifier for the "number" label, like a sort-of "number.getAddress()" call. The & is applied to the label "number" in order to tell the compiler "I don't want the contained int value itself, I want the address in memory where the int value is located".

And if you have an address stored somewhere, you can de-reference it by using the * modifier. So say you have your "&number" result (i.e. the memory address) stored in a variable with the label "address", then you apply the * modifier to the "address" label to tell the compiler "I don't care about the address, I want the value it's storing", like a quasi "address.getContent()" call. And as a result, such a * modifier call will return the integer value hiding behind the de-referenced address.

So when de-referencing, the * symbol is not part of a data type, but a modifier to what the "address" label stands for, i.e. a modifier for the address it stores. And the data type of the "return value" of the memory-address-getter "&" is not an int, but a pointer to a memory address. These are two very important sentence for my case. The * and & symbols are MODIFIERS to the LABELS, they are NOT DATA TYPES of the returned VALUE.

Let's consider declaring a variable that will contain the memory address of an integer container somewhere in memory. Even if the integer type is just a tiny 8-bit int8_t, the memory addressing in 64-bit systems requires 64 bits of memory to store memory addresses. So storing the address of an 8-bit integer will require 64 bits of memory, which means the pointer can not be an 8-bit int8_t i.e. you would - or rather could - NOT declare it as "int8_t address = &number;" because the 8 bits of the int8_t would not suffice to store the 64-bit memory address returned from the & modifier.

In other words: the int8_t before the label "address" has nothing to do with the address itself, but it's a hint to what the data AT the stored address will be interpreted as, and how many Bytes of memory it actually has covered. But ... since the address we're storing is not the int8_t value in "number" itself, but the address to it, and the & modifier returns the data type "pointer to int8_t", the only sensible way of notation is to add the * symbol in the declaration to the int8_t mention - because it's part of the data type of the "address" label.

The "address" label is a  "pointer to an int8_t  container", so the only rationally sensible way to declare it is "int8_t* address = &number;". Because, as explained earlier on, writing the * symbol immediately before the label suggests it's the de-referencing modifier. If you declare your variable "int8_t *address = &number;" it would suggest that you think the * modifies the "address" label, which is not the case. So it would be irrational and unsensible to use it there.

And if you pass an argument into a function by reference, the & is NOT a modifier to the label of the variable, but again - like the * in a pointer variable - part of the data type of the variable/label. Adding an argument as "std::vector<double> &numbers" would suggest that the & symbol is applied to the "numbers" label as a modifier, which obviously isn't the case. The & should go where it belongs, and that is left to the data type, as in "std::vector<double>& numbers", because that's the only rationally sensible place to put it. The label "numbers" will contain a reference to a double-vector. The argument label "numbers" is not modified by the & symbol at all, so why suggest it should be.

double number = 8.0;
double* address = &number;
double alsoNumber = *address;
void useNum (const double& NumReference, double* NumPointer) 
{ std::cout << "Reference: " << NumReference << ", Pointer: " << *NumPointer << -std::endl- '\n';}

That's the only sensible way to place those symbols. Anything else would be ludicrous and completely illogical. Even if we all know how to interpret them correctly, it takes extra time to make this *gong* newbie habits.

Writing things like "for (const auto pair.getAddress() : colors)" wouldn't make a lot of sense now, would it? So why write it that way? If you want the pair to be of a referenced data type, the PUT THE & WHERE THE DATA TYPE IS, i.e. "for (const auto& pair : colors)", because that's the only way it makes sense. :)

Thank your for your attention. If you all implement my reasoning in your code, you will all make the world a better place.

author: @sertunc-k5o
text:
To those who are just beginning their journey in software development, I’d like to offer a humble suggestion; Programming languages are ultimately just tools — not the goal itself. The language you choose should depend on the problem you're trying to solve. You select the appropriate tool, study its documentation, learn it, and apply it as needed.

But more important than mastering a specific language is developing strong problem-solving skills and learning how to approach problems methodically. For this reason, I recommend that you first build a solid understanding of algorithms and programming logic before diving deep into any particular language.

And by “algorithms,” I don't just mean sorting or searching algorithms — I mean the ability to think through and design the logical flow of tasks in any given software. Writing code is a result; without proper planning and a thoughtful approach, creating efficient and maintainable solutions becomes quite difficult.
Start your software journey with strong foundations.
With respect and best wishes

author: @rassman48
text:
It started with nonsense, Can't call yourself professional with only one4 language? 
I am sure we all know that we only tried each language as it came out to see if it added something or if it made the developer's life easier. It rarely did either of those.

Starting with assembler, you built up massive libraries of macros and procedures, so when the first decent looking C came along, I could still knock together software with my assembler/macros faster than I could using early C, and I knew there was no hidden code.

Pascal was always too much typing. 
Ada was wonderful, had to use it for most military stuff, but still out side the military I could still knock together an assembler prog quicker.

However, when C6 happened that changed everything, I know C6 was an environment rather than a language in it's own right, but it was the only thing that tempted me away from assembler, for a lot of years I was still a heavy mix of assembler and C, but you learn to trust the C part in time, so that took over. 

And frankly I would not have moved on from there if the contract work didn't insist on using the latest thing that their IT department had bought. Don't tell anyone, but when I had to do some freaky OOPs work, I used my own lib files to do most of the work and pretty much ignored as much of the oops as I possibly could.

One other thing came along, C#. I thought from the start that it was the direction C was always meant to go. Ok so the early years you kept crashing into stack size problems. But it isn't like that now, I don't know off the top of my head what it's current limits are, but I know I haven't bumped into any of them.

C++: The language has strict static typing. The code attempts to push a string literal "2" into a std::vector<int> (vector of integers). This is a type mismatch that the compiler will catch, resulting in a compilation error.

text:
I think people talking about "speed" are not asking though "What is an int and string type doing in the same container?" 

I know this is Python, and that's a thing you can do. It's just what should it do? Should it print the integer 1 in C++ or should the string 2 be converted into the integer 2 or should the mix of two types be allowed?

At the end of this Python script, there's a backend doing the heavy lifting for you. If you wanted this behavior, you can code it yourself in C++ but the problem is, what do you use this for and why would you need it? You'll trade something to acquire it, and in Python, you'll basically see that. Mix in large number of types or mix in a larger data set, what happens to performance? What happens to memory? 

These are things you don't think about with Python, because often you're understanding the need to trade convenience for speed is the goal, and that's a good thing sometimes, and why Python is fine, but not always needed in all case.

author: @octalide4863
text:
I'm really not sure why so many people like rust. I despise the syntactical sugar sprinkled around the language all in the name of memory safety. It completely sacrifices readability and writing speed for that functionally negligible performance increase (I say functionally negligible because, while rust IS faster than many languages, the speed difference won't be relevant unless the author is writing the code for a real time system (no, NOT your game engine -- think microcontrollers in ECUs, where nanoseconds are essential). A good example of this in practice is the simple fact that C# game engines exist. C# is a MUCH slower language than rust in many ways AND is garbage collected, but can still perform well enough to power AAA games.

Those reasons alone are enough for me to far prefer something like go over rust -- golang being a language that is "minified" while managing to be extremely capable, performant, easy to write with, AND garbage collected (the GC is extremely efficient and can be configured or even turned off in special cases). I would much rather write code in another language than fight the rust compiler over memory management, wacky syntax, and an arbitrage of single-use keywords for functionality that simply does not need to be included in the base library of a language.

TLDR; IMHO rust is the wrong language unless you're writing a kernel or embedded code and don't want to use C. I dislike it very much.

author: @oconnor663
text:
> mutable values...are stored in the heap

This is incorrect, and it's a pretty fundamental point. Rust is happy to have mutable values on the stack. The stack vs heap distinction in Rust is similar to the same in C++: objects need to live on the heap if their size is unknown at compile time (as the video mentions) or if their lifetime isn't limited to any particular scope. In Rust this is often done with Vec, Box, or Arc, much like C++ would use vector, unique_ptr, or shared_ptr.

Rust's unique approach to mutability is unrelated to the stack/heap distinction. The rule in Rust is that a mutable object can't be aliased; there can only be a single, unique reference to it while it's being mutated. This dovetails very closely with the ownership and borrowing rules that keep track of object lifetimes and prevent use-after-free bugs. These are the parts of Rust that make it really unique.

Man, I still have my plans for my GSD language...  The cold compile times would be atrocious, but great incremental, and such great unorthodox features, people would either love it, or just be too confused by it being too alien...
GSD stands for:  _Getting Shit Done_
- The main thing I want is a heavy consistent suport for compile time evaluation, which all languages need (macros, templates,...), but it's rarely elevated to a first class citizen. Instead it should be the basis.

Sorry, I have to be that guy.

1. The example C++ code is very contrived, you rarely use malloc and free in C++ (like you would in C) because...
2. C++ uses RAII. Necessary heap memory is allocated when the object is created, and freed when the object falls out of scope. The same system is used in Rust.
3. Just because something is variable, does not mean it is stored on the heap. If it's size does not change over the program's lifetime, there is no reason to allocate it on the heap. For example: a mutable u32 is initialized to 0, and later changed to 5. This u32 does not need to be on the heap, because no matter what it's value is, it will always have a size of 32 bits.

author: @necauqua
text:
You never said a thing about 'unsafe' and safe abstractions around unsafe code, it's a big part of Rust imo

---

So many people are saying that whether the variable is stored on the stack or on the heap based on if it's Sized (has a known compile-time size) or not.
THIS IS WRONG, OMG PEOPLE!
You just cannot directly create a variable with an unsized type, because all the variables you create have live on the stack.

What you _do_ have to do to create a variable on the heap is to use a Box - a smart pointer which stores the data on the heap, and the box itself (which is just a pointer with extra drop behavior to deallocate) instead lives on the stack.

Same thing with all the collections (like Vec) and other smart pointers (e.g. Rc) - you create it on the stack and it will allocate memory on the heap (you can write your own with a Box, but the std one has a bunch of 'unsafe' optimizations with a safe public interface) and contain a pointer to that memory within itself and use it to store data.

author: @scheimong
text:
Normally I like every video you make but I'll make an exception to this one. The few errors you made here can be very misleading to someone just starting out.

First, `let mut` does not put a variable on the heap; `Box::new` (or other smart pointers) does. Someone else already explained it so I'll pass.
Second, "mut" is not pronounced with a flat "u" (as in "mud"), instead say it the same way you would say the full word "mutable". This is a minor issue but nonetheless.
Finally, for most use cases you *really* shouldn't be using rustc directly. Instead use `cargo build --release` and `cargo run --release`, which is not only easier but also compiles your dependencies.

Granted Rust is particularly complex and 100 seconds is a short time. But I feel like this video could use some more research and is not up to your usual standards in the current state.

author: @Speykious
text:
Despite Rust being my favorite programming language, it has 2 major problems:
- its ecosystem of external libraries is quite immature, and there is still a lot of improvement on the line.
- it *statically* links its standard library by default, which is a huge issue for the disk space that your executable will take. This way, every program, _even one that just has an empty main function,_ will take at least 3 megabytes of disk space.
Now of course there is the `-C prefer-dynamic` flag on rustc to compile the program with dynamic linking, but now at least you know that it's not the default.

author: @pavelperina7629
text: I don't know. I tried to rewrite one a rather simple Python program when speed matter into Julia and Rust just for curiosity. I found Rust more logical to a certain point ... when I needed to access buffer (image) by columns from multiple threads. At this point, it became a nightmare and not using programing language as a tool, but instead fighting with it's limitations or safety features. Also Julia had libraries I needed and nicer syntax for a lot of math, where rust has function written after the expression, not before, so it's hardly readable. I'm not saying Julia was without problems - threaded loop sharing mutable variables without strong typing was slow, but with everything made typed and constant it became ten times faster (still twice slower than Rust, but 100-500x faster than Python). But I'm not convinced that Rust is a language I want to use. I'd like to have something like C++ that solves dependencies without a need to spend hours writing CMake files. Memory safety? Since we have shared_ptr and unique_ptr, I don't feel like it's a major problem. Avoiding deadlocks and writing highly parallel that does not spend time by waiting is.

author: @stanislausbrown8626
text:
That was actually a very reasonable video. I like that you are not strident. 

Yes, it's important to be exposed to several languages, not just in a classroom settings, but in an actual work environment.

I remember the Java craze when everybody said it would take over the world. I have precisely one Java program that I keep around on my machine - one, after thirty years in IT.

I'm sure C++ has its use cases but I've also heard that it can be difficult to debug because of all the class libraries. I suppose that can be true of any object oriented programming language.

Javascript is now all the rage but it suffers from depending on things other people somewhere else on the net may have written. 

I remember a case where a programmer pulled his code from a repo and an amazing amount of Javascript applications crashed because one obscure function in his code disappeared. That's a vulnerability no one expected.

I liked the Fortan example. I've never written any Fortran myself but I do appreciate that older languages have had more time to mature and become highly optimized.

I kinda like PHP. It's certainly easy to use. I've used it as a scripting language for applications that have nothing to do with the web.

But something I find that programmers, in general, overlook, is programming for maintainability.

 Good programs can last for decades. And the first thing that happens to a good program, is that it constantly gets modified. 

People always want customisation, reports, changes to screens, workflow, new features, etc.

There's a big difference between programs designed to be maintained over a long period of time versus something written quickly to solve an immediate problem. 

C++ was developed because of the problem of maintaining huge programs over long periods of time. 

PHP was not. It has always been a quick-and-dirty-fix-it-now kind of language. Though it has improved over time. And despite its warts, it is used in a lot of websites, including Facebook.

author: @agugyin
text: According to the creator of C++, it is a "language design language". Just keep that in mind. C++ is BIG and layered. Probably bigger than anything one would need for solving a particular problem, but that also means it's universal, most versatile and definitely not dead. However thinking big as Stroustrup is insane for anyone without at least 5 years of C coding experience IMO. C is the best systems programming language (enough for a lot of structuring and organizing a system - an automation tool, industrial control/monitor equipment, embedded computer, instrument/controller device, inter-device device, so, many things - from a hardware perspective) for nearly any "living" hardware out there, regardless of infrastructure, yet with the "roll your own" driver feel that of Unix/Linux systems, which other OSes hide and outsource from the developer. C++ stems from that and takes it to a very high level, yet, the use of C++ is rarely reaching this proposed level of abstraction. C++ tries to maintain the reach to the underlying system while being more application-friendly with advanced safety and security considerations, but that won't stop beginner programmers to break the rules unknowingly (it shouldn't be a surprise that most operating systems come with tons of non-standard versions and language extensions as hardware development is very out of sync with the development of the C++ standard and yes, this breeds legacy bloatware as adaptation of new tech is faster than standardization and spread of its concepts and uses). In a way, the option of bringing computer language closer to say, technical English is already available with the C preprocessor and its standard library. C++ on the other hand is for modeling and designing much less hardware-dependent software on top of already present OS/network infrastructure. That goes with a lot of extra work and newer languages with their dependencies already carried out by newer technologies (virtual machines, containers, advanced internet protocols and lots of processes hardly relatable for non-engineering disciplines) make using C++ seem obsolete - yet it's still almost everywhere. I think (rather believe :)) C++ is for the highly literate who are ready for never coming out of the rabbit hole but keep in mind that some *customers* write *specifications* in C (that's direct experience, don't ask, why :D).

author: @DysoniaMultiverseNews
text:
I agree a lot with the key message of this video. It really doesn't matter which languages to learn so much. Sure, there are jobs listing the languages they are looking for job applicants to have. Your wage or salary is not so much about what languages you know but your education, knowledge, experience and ability. So it's that experience and ability to deliver. The languages they point to is for what they (employers) are working with and using and sometimes they just aren't ready to re-do what they had already invested in.... the issues of 'legacy' software. 

Now, when I began programming, I was working with BASIC and Assembly/Machine Language for various CPUs and computer hardware platforms such as 6502 based systems (including 65c816 CPUs and microcontrollers, etc.), TMS9900 from Texas Instruments (used in TI-99/4 and 4A), 68K series, 8080/z80, 8086 through  286 and some additional stuff with 386/486 and Pentium but these later x86 systems to present, I would use languages such as C and C++ and other languages that often have compilers to produce decent performant code. For performance, back in the earlier days, programming in machine language was the best with highly tuned programming. Back then, C++ didn't yet exist in the public commercial tools in the microcomputers era. Around mid-80s, we started to see C. Then C++ was emerging around 1990. C++ was not very beneficial for 8 bit systems and it was in the 16/32 bit era that we saw the emergence of C and C++. There was a few C compilers for C but it's code was only okay but machine language code can be more performant. 6502 machine language wasn't that hard to learn. However, modern CPUs have much more complex instruction set so it was easier to program in C and C++ and other high level languages that would compile. As C/C++ compilers evolved with optimization features, the code would be performant and as computers also got faster, the time and effort to code in machine code on the newer and faster computers was quickly becoming a waste of time for highly advanced code. Over the years, I have learned the myriad of languages including QuickBASIC/QBasic, Visual Basic, Java, various web-oriented scripting/programming/etc. languages such as HTML, CSS, XML, DHTML, XHTML, PHP, PERL, Javascript,  and newer stuff like Dart (with Flutter), Typescript, AssemblyScript / WebAssembly, more modern C++, etc. The languages are a long list, so it's matters to understand the software engineering principles and applying them regardless of the languages. The point of using the right tool for the work at hand that meets the requirements and that you can adequately deliver with less work because that is what employers are going to look for... time is money after all. 

If you can do the job in a language that meets the requirements that you know well enough to do it in 6 months but you would have to spend 12+ months in another adequate language that meets requirements, its fairly clear what language to use.... under most employment situations, the one that requires less time is what you would be expected to use. There's real world practical considerations. 

In my experience, a lot of the languages I have experience in are now obsolete in any work situations but I can tell you C/C++ is one of those languages that have stood the test of time. 

Stefan, good job with the video.

author: @skilz8098
text:
It is a leading language in many fields but that is determined by the environment you are working in. It's based on context. In other words, in some trade areas it is the goto language, but it's not the leading language for every scenario. It depends on the type of job or project you are working with. If you're writing a compiler, drivers or operating systems code, game engine development, hardware emulation, avionics, navigational systems, audio and signal processing then yes languages like C and C++ are probably the better fit. A lot of your lower end boilerplate code for servers and databases again C and C++, not always but is still a good choice. If you're doing basic and simple desktop applications it still has its place as does many other languages. Now once you get to the more abstracted areas such as web development, user interfaces, etc... then other languages like C#, F#, Java, JavaScript, Python, Pearl, Ruby, Rust, etc... are probably more practical. It depends on the requirements of the application's primary tasks and goals. If it is data driven crunching through a lot of data performing high volumes of calculations with efficiency and little overhead in mind as well as wanting it to be portable, generic, modular, and maintainable code such as libraries or interfaces then C / C++ are very good choices. If the code is user event or I/O driven and there are many calls back across the bus where there is going to be known delays, then other languages like C#, Java, JavaScript and Python are probably better. If it is task driven with repeatable tasks then shell languages would be a good fit. If you're doing A.I. or Machine Learning then C/C++ Python and a few others are all good choices. It all depends on the requirements and specification of the job as well as the already existing infrastructures. In many cases it is a leading language and in many other cases it is not. Knowing what the appropriate language is for the task at hand is more important than C++ being the #1 or #5 language of choice. One thing that does make C++ so powerful today isn't just its speed and efficiency, it's also the plethora of libraries that are already out there for you to integrate into your existing code base pending on licenses and permissions. 

I'm 100% self taught in C++ since around 2003-05. I started with C++ when I taught myself how to use DirectX and OpenGL, and these days I started to pick up a little bit of Vulkan. I've never worked in the field as I have done this as a hobby, yet I have very decent to a very good understanding of how the business and industry standards are. When a company invest millions into a specific platform and language and they're offering you work you will have to adapt to their environment. They're not going to switch from one format to another on the drop of a dime just because you're better at one language than another or because another language might be better for the job than the one they're using. Now in some cases if a language becomes "dead" or if the entire original code base is so old that no one knows that language and there's no one left around who originally wrote it to explain it, then they might consider updating their systems to a new format. A good rule of thumb would be to know programming concepts more than a language as that is your trade and from there to know maybe 3-5 of the most commonly used languages as tools in your tool kits. 

What do you think is more important? Your ability to read and write C syntax, SQL syntax, Lisp syntax? Or is it your ability to understand containers, algorithms (sort, search, find and replace, etc...), space and time complexities, object lifetime and memory management, thread safety, compression and decompression algorithms, encryption and decryption, file parsing, version control, project management, etc? Again which of the two do you think is more important? A language can easily be picked up and learned switching it out for another. The ability to derive well structured algorithms through Pseudocode is much more valuable. If you're not sure what the Pseudocode is meant or is going to do what makes you think you're going to be able to instruct the computer to properly do it for you in an efficient and precise manner? 

When you start to excel beyond that is when you'll begin to start making your own tools!  Here's an example, there's a game developer who left the mainstream or AAA developer studios that used C++ as a primary language and there were some things he liked about it but there was a lot that he didn't. On his own time, he decided to write his own programming language that is slightly similar to C++ in some ways but far different as it was geared to be a language specific to game programming. He removed a lot of the overhead from various components, added in capabilities the language didn't have to offer, etc... and from that he started to make his own games. One of the latest games that I'm aware of that he written and designed is called The Witness. Understand the Hardware and how it works to better know how to get it what you want it to do! In your spare time, trying writing a few novel programs in Assembly, or try to write a program in the language of your choice that will act as a CPU with its registers, cache, instructions, etc. and design your own ISA and your own Assembler. That'll truly strengthen your skills more than any one language can! And I'm just a Hobbyist!

author: @ruffianeo3418
text:
Does 25-ish years of C++ programming count as experienced? Well - I mostly used it in embedded programming as a less error prone and more productive alternative to C (and the C fanboys never liked it). On the desktop, my embedded software also ran in test beds (software in the loop) as one step towards running it on the embedded targets (which varied frequently in terms of OS and hardware platform). 
For Tooling on the PC (stuff like generating code or configuration apps or test systems), we opted for the highest level language which also worked fine for GUI programming (was C# back then, nowadays, I would go with F# or Common Lisp).
At that point I started screening for alternatives (did not like C++11 and what came after (C++17 was more to my taste, eventually)) and I did a language tour, including the hyped functional languages (like Haskell). And to my surprise, what I now use for my explorative, prototyping, proof of concept and tooling language is none of the fancy new languages but Common Lisp. Why? High Level AND fast (if you aim for fast). 

For embedded (and probably server side programming), Rust looks like an alternative if people can accept the slow tool chain (it also does a lot a C compiler does not... but still) and really want applications which have higher prospect of being reliable.

The one language I never used and probably never will (unless you pay me triple :)) is Python. The syntax makes my eyes sore and it is slow. So why would I use it if instead I can use Lisp which is closer to C speed and once you got used to it, the syntax makes sense. Python is still in the uncanny valley, performance wise - comparable to interpreted lisps of the era between 1958 and 1990 (after, Common Lisp was more a compiled language than an interpreted one).

If there was more financial and support power behind OCAML, it very well could be the high level language of choice. But sometimes it feels as if it is maintained by just 3 dudes in a basement... And when I benchmarked ocamlopt compiled ocaml, it was slower than F# on .NET core. So I moved on.

author: @gogobram
text:
Every programming has a natural lifecycle.

How languages respond to innovation depends on the size of the community. If the community is small, they will redesign to make it blend in the way it should, keeping it compact. If the community is large, they will add a backwards compatible extension, making the language bigger.

The result is that old languages become feature-rich but ugly. While young languages stay slim and accessible.

And then at some stage, the community reaches its maximum size because it becomes easier to rewrite, then to learn it. It gets harder to recruit employees, but there's money to spend. So, then a rewrite happens, or it gets split in multiple applications in different languages.

A nice example is how XML and SOAP got replaced by JSON and REST. Even though XML and SOAP are way more powerful, they are also way more complicated. It just got too difficult to learn.

C/C++ is a systems programming language, which goes as close to the hardware level as possible, without actually being assembler language. I get why many people hate C++, especially if they have a background with other programming languages. The syntax is often ugly and hard to read, meta programming is full of nasty traps and it can be cryptic; surprising semantics, often involving surprising implicit casting. And it just has way too many features; I often refer to C++ as a huge pile of misguided features -- even experts are often surprised that you could do this or that. 

Obviously, none of this is irrepareable, but the resulting language would be something very different. I think Rust and D are very sensible contenders.

author: @haroldmcbroom7807
text:
You can't always trust the "industry", as the "industry" is somewhat of a tight knit group, when one corporation has a "good ideal" others are quick to jump on the bandwagon.   They lack passion, and care only for $$$.    They set the standards by which everyone else is dumbed down, and they control the industry, so that no individual person can create something that makes them look STUPID.  I'm 51 years old, and I've grown with the gaming industry since the mid-80's, and I can say that today, the gaming industry feels DEAD, because of "cross-platform" programming, or "migration" as I like to call it, "Early Access" development which allows developers to get paid before the game reaches completion, while not being under and obligation to complete the games, small 1 to 2 or more member development teams which lack the experience to optimize their own games.   And this is just the software side of things, next comes the hardware side, where companies are making computers using cheap components that break down; it's as though the industry is being intentionally sabotaged by those who want to control "technology and information".

I was told that it was a bad ideal for new developers to create their own "game engines" from the start, and that they should learn existing game engines, how they work, and to become proficient, once they have gained experience in creating games,  and have the money and expertise, only then should they consider creating their own "gaming engines".  Another reason, is because it takes a lot of money to create a game engine, an top of that, the high cost of developing the actual game which utilizes the game engine.

To be honest, I have two years in Business Programming, where I was taught C++, COBOL, Pascal, and BASIC, but I was *NOT* taught the CORRECT way to program as is found in the REAL WORLD, when you examine professional C programs such as those by the popular YouTuber "Bisqwit", who is a sheer genius.   I was only taught the basic syntax of the languages, and introduced to "hello world" type programs.   I had no ideal before I attended Interactive Learning Systems, that "no one is going to hire an entry level programmer", and to be further honest, I wouldn't have even hired myself.  When you want to create the best game in the world, no one wants to hire entry level programmer, but someone who knows their stuff.

My education wasn't a total waste.  It's true, that if you know one language you can easily learn others, with a few exceptions.  No matter how good you are in COBOL will never prepare you for Assembly Language.  My knowledge of BASIC, allowed me to quickly learn Excel VBA, in which I was able to take a job being performed by 3 different people, sometimes had help from others, working 8 hours a day, write a program that did the job in 3 to 4 minutes.   It was the difference between hiring a data entry person, and hiring a data entry person with programming knowledge.

If you're new to programming, and want to be a developer, or even somewhat experienced, but do not have a premium license, then you'll go through "toolchain hell", trying to find a free compiler with IDE, along with third-party graphics libraries.   Back in the day when I was learning, we were given everything we needed, including graphics libraries.   You'll run into so many problems now days, from "free compilers" that are no longer being worked on, or that have migrated under new names, to issues installing them, once you install them, then you have to fight over getting the third-party IDE to work with said compiler, and once you've banged your head on your desk with THAT, then comes that point that you press F1 for help, and there are no help files installed.   It almost feels as though they do not want us to learn anything for free on the internet.

It wasn't my vocational school that taught me anything, but the books I bought from Herbert Schildt of Mcgraw Hill who wrote books such as "Teach Yourself C++", etc.   First off I owe GOD for giving me the ability to understand these things, and I appreciate Herbert for all of his wonderful books.

text:
C++ is a bad language. It does not offer memory protection and lets any contributor to a big project to crash it entirely. It has very complicated syntax with many many many hidden traps you gradually discover as you try to design more complex things.
It carries stone-age legacy of C.
Standard C library within C++ is ancient. Standard Template Library also carries 90s legacy and gives subpar performance. Fortunately, some of this is fixed in C++20 with ranges.
C/C++ are designed to support many more CPUs than you care about and as result define no fixed length and no standard representation for, say, signed integers. If you rely on ints being 32 bits, or on 2-complement representation,  a compiler may punish you severely, often without a warning. C/C++ standards are full of Implementation-Defined and Undefined Behavior.
With C++ you spend more time fighting the language, deciphering cryptic errors, making workarounds for specific compilers, than solving actual problems.

author: @meatgoat4084
text:
Still so much misinformation here.

C++ was my first and forever love.  My life with it began in college in 1989 with cfront.  My first paying C++ job was in 1993 with AT&T C++ in the telecom industry.  My most recent C++ job was less than a year ago in the enterprise storage industry.  I've worked closely with C++ over the course of many jobs (including within the game industry) through all of its generations over a span of 31 years and I consider it my most marketable skill.  But throughout that time I've also had years of experience with C, C#, Java, Scala, and Python, and I'm currently having to become proficient with Go.  None of those have been by my personal choice but were required of the jobs that I've chosen to accept.

The bottom line is there is no "choosing a language" if you want to be a professional software developer.  That is a phoney meme promulgated by non-practitioners.  In the end you'll be expected to do whatever the job you've accepted demands from you.  So people entering the career should be more concerned with "choosing the right job in the right industry".  Developers who are happy in one industry may be completely miserable in others.

I know that the hiring process for developers is badly broken.  Believe me, I've been battling this condition for many years.  There is some truth to the accusation that resumes and CVs are screened for certain magic phrases, again by non-practitioners.

But, when you get past those levels of idiocy you will at some point have to impress actual practitioners.  That's when you will find your "choice of language" is not very important.  More important will be your proficiency and competency within the technology ecosystem that surrounds particular languages.  For example, I can easily determine your proficiency with Java by probing your knowledge of JVM performance, how you engineer your build and test environments, and how you engineer integrations with the outside world, without asking you a single question about Java syntax.  If you can't provide satisfactory answers to those concerns then your knowledge of language specifics is not going to impress me.  The same goes for C++, Python, C#, and anything else.  Each language is surrounded by an even more important ecosystem of supporting packages and libraries, tools, patterns and practices, and cultures.

So, how do you spot the practitioner poser?  When they confidently reply to the question "what language should I learn?" by actually naming a language.

As a self-taught C Programmer that practically knows A->Z of all Computing, I think most 'Programmers' doesn't fully grasp the meaning of 'C is everywhere' and for what I know, in consequence to what Linus Torvalds meant with 'I have yet to see a language that comes even close to C in that respect'.. And hence throw the pun of "Why don't you write it in assembly?".

Assembly is a Human Readable syntax for Machine Code, this is why you can't actually say 'Oh it's in Assembly' and must specify the Architecture and even Architecture Version.

C is a Human Readable syntax for Assembly the same way Assembly is a Human Readable syntax for Machine code.. But now, you do not have to worry about the Architecture and can actually do proper work.

You use Assembly to not worry about Binary specifics, you use C to not have to worry about Architecture specifics.. You use Rust to not have to worry about Memory Order and you use something alike Python to not have to worry about Programming and hence, Python is a Coding Language - You configure requirements instead of instructing operations..

author: @ColeLeytem
text:
However, "better" depends on your goals—safer code, easier concurrency, modularity, or even AI-assisted development in the future. 

C's Weaknesses: 
Manual Memory Management, Lack of Type Safety and Bounds Checking, Concurrency Issues, Undefined Behavior (UB), Portability Pitfalls, Error-Prone Macros and Preprocessor, Security Risks.

These weaknesses contribute to the fact that a huge percentage of CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) in OS kernels stem from C code. Linux kernel devs spend tons of time hunting memory bugs.

Existing Alternatives to C for OS Development:
 Rust, Zig, Ada/SPARK, Go, C++.

Experimental/Future-Oriented: Languages like Vale (with region-based memory) or Carbon (Google's C++ successor) could evolve for OS work. In the 2030s+, we might see languages with built-in AI verification or quantum-safe features.
These show it's not just possible—it's happening. 😎

The worst Java code I've ever seen was part of (Googles) easier mediapipe API.

Combine that with the need to also use the not easy and not well documented camera2 API (which they combined with some parts of CameraX) and that under all that Spagetti mess they used JNI to call C++ code that also wasn't particularly well documented, and I got nowhere but sure wasted a lot of time thinking I finally got to the target.

Honestly, while we're at this, LARGE swaths of the Android API require you to use implementation Inheritance, so thanks for forcing me to do the things you forbid your engineers to do Google.

Sorry for the rant, I'm still super salty from that experience. What they archived with mediapipe is remarkable, and it's nice they made it open source. But mediapipe did not keep it's promises (real time body tracking on IOT, pretty much every mobile - top models released after mediapipe - we tried didn't get over sustained 10 FPS, while being at best at a mean of 18 FPS), and the API was a nightmare and not at all flexible enough for our needs.

author: @haxney
text:
Great video!

A few things, from a Google engineer (not speaking for the whole company, of course).

1. We absolutely have tech debt. These things help reduce certain kinds of tech debt, but it still exists all over the place. We're not magical; we make bad choices which we're then stuck with.

2. The lexical code style goes beyond just tabs vs spaces. Our code review system will yell at you if the code isn't formatted according to whatever clang-format would produce. Our style guide for indentation, line breaks, etc, is just "run clang-format and use that". I don't always like the choices which clang-format makes, but it's infinitely better for everyone to use the same standard than for me to use a standard I like more, but for diffs to be larger due to whitespace changes.

3. An important part of the style guide boils down to "don't get clever with template metaprogramming." I've been writing C++ for about 3 years now, and as soon as things get beyond the most basic template usage, I'm lost. If you're relying on SFINAE, you should probably reach for a different solution. Same thing once you start dealing with rvalues and lvalues. There are some places where those features really do make sense, but for things like "call this service. If foo is greater than 25, set bar to true", you probably don't need that stuff.

Since children in real life don't inherit everything evenly and directly from both parents, it doesn't make any sense to define their classes like that. author: @kennethgee2004
text:
so that last part is to follow SOLID design.  Each class holds unique concerns, and use composition over inheritance, so that functions and responsibilities stay separated.  Inheritance has its place, but is not engineered correctly.  With classes that mainly hold data and handle some transformations inheritance is not well suited.  For objects that build upon each other like window systems, then behavioral design there says that inheritance is good.  

With all of this said it is impossible to write debt free code.  We are developers.  The use of tabs should be encouraged.  Set your editors as a preference.  We engineer differently and have unique styles.  Some solutions are only found when people can be themselves.  All of this will lead to debt though in the sees of style.  

The issue here of debt free code is not the style of coding that one uses.  The issue is how to engineer properly.  This video touched on using interfaces.  Interfaces are really important and needed in all projects.  We should be designing for interfaces as that allows for modularity.  Need a new way to access data?  Not an issue as along as the data access returns all of the correct data sets.  Which data sets are there well that is where an interface comes in, as the functions should be set based on the business logic necessary to run the front end.  In this way we can reduce debt as we are only changing one concern at a time.  Debt is not style, but failings in logic. 

I also disagree with the non-use of exceptions.  Exceptions are not just program breaks, but are failures in design, and should be looked into.  Without the exception we have no idea why the program just crashed.  What is needed is a better way to handle logging.  They will need a standard library for logging exceptions.  It is now each concerns responsibility to report the error to the logging and then handle the exception per the concern.  In the example in the video the function g handles no exceptions from H or more likely handles errors in H by raising the exception again, which passes it up to F.  This is an example of poor design.  where is the separation of concern?  if function F is the concern and functions G and H only perform data manipulation, then the responsibility for error is at function F.  if each function is its own concern, then we need a way to decouple these nested calls.

Google demonstrated a bunch of epic fails in its style guide.
A relatively simple question around tabs vs spaces should definitely be answered in favor of tabs.
The tab width of a single character MUST be different from one engineer to another because each engineer is comfortable with his/her own tab width.
What has Google achieved with its 2 spaces?
The most of engineers are uncomfortable with the view of code except those who are comfortable with 2 spaces.
In both cases the code is the same among all the engineers, but in case of 2 spaces the most of engineers are uncomfortable with the code.
What a great accomplishment!
Google does not use exceptions and this is an extremely dramatic fail in its style guide.
Imagine a situation when a variable of some class is created, a constructor of that class is called and it finds out during construction that the object cannot be constructed.
For example, because of a temporary lack of resources needed for the construction.
How could I find out that the variable cannot be used then in the code after its definition, because it is not constructed completely?
The only way a constructor can notify the code after the variable definition that the variable has not been constructed is to throw an exception.
Another situation: imagine I use a custom allocator for std::vector.
How can the allocator notify the code working with a std::vector object that the space for more elements cannot be allocated?
And finally, perhaps you will be laughing but the standard library throws exceptions too.
So what?
Not to use the standard library?
Really?
Try to find a fail that is more epic than that of Google in its design of not to use exceptions at all in their style guide.
That is why they even made an attempt to return to using exceptions but it is already too-too late and therefore they have failed even with that...

author: @ov3rcl0cked
text:
I follow this inheritance rule in pretty much every language. Unless it's a clear cut case where inheritance makes the most sense, in terms of sharing a lot of code,  I'll opt for interfaces. I'll also prevent multiple layers of inheritance. I feel like the further you come from the base class then more confusing and implicit things can become. You end up not really knowing what the class is composed of. I instead will often look to encapsulation, and usually dependency injecting these encapsulated pieces, because it's also astonishingly easier to test. I have no strict rule around this, but I feel like if you're 5 layers of inheritance deep you're usually shooting yourself in the foot. I feel like many developers stray away from encapsulation when they can use inheritance, like one is somehow intrinsically better than the other.

A trick I've come to like when things start to get complicated with inheritance is to create an interface that defines all common methods, in C++ this would be a purely abstract class, and then have a base class for any common pieces to inherit. So in the case of a mother, father, and child, the parents might have their own base class which implements the interface, and child would just implement the interface, and maybe child could encapsulate a reference to the parents. This way any similarities in implementation the child shares with either parent is also specific to the instance of their parents. Child could even have it's own base class and you could create daughter and son, where maybe they each emphasize the characteristics of the parent who has the same sex as them, given this isn't how it actually works but serves the analogy.

I really see inheritance as mechanism to not repeat yourself, but I often see people trying to think of it too literally. Like the example mother, father, child, the child obviously literally inherits the mother and father, but you're kind of abusing the programming term "inheritance" to mean something it really doesn't. The child CLASS doesn't inherit traits from the parent CLASSES, it inherits PROPERTIES from a given INSTANCE of it's parents. Java doesn't allow multiple inheritance, and I honestly feel like that's prevented a lot of mishaps. On the other hand, I've dealt with inheritance nightmares in Pythons. I've seen a lot of people who abuse inheritance. We had a network protocol that had a major change between version 1 and 2, and the original developer implemented a base class to handle all the lower level networking pieces, many of which were common among version 1 and 2, and then inherited that into the v1 client. That's all well and good, but the real mind bender is the fact that they inherited the v1 client into the v2 client. Wild. It was so hard figuring out what happened where, and why these 2 major versions had overlapping code bases. It was a nightmare to pull that apart. This guy actually now works at Google, though I'm sure they've taught him a few lessons.

text: I wonder how "exception free" code should work. If you get an error in a highly specialized simple function, you very often simply can't handle it there in a meaningful way. Well you could always return some kind of error status, but I'd expect this gets more and more complicated as it "travels" up to the call chain to a function that actually can deal with it and is in end a poor own implemention of the exception mechanism. Also if you use an external library, you've to deal with exceptions coming from there anyway. When it comes to inheritance, just stick with a single parent and you should be fine. You can not just replace inheritance with interfaces because you would have to re-implement the functionality every time you use an interface where normally you would rely on the existing implementation of a parent class. You could separate functionality from data and have classes that only have functions and that accept instances of other classes as parameter to work on their data but I'm sure that this would increase the overall complexity by a lot for no apparent reason.

author: @rashifr
text:
You never inherit something like Child from Father and Mother. Or Car from Engine. Those are clear compositions. Think "has-a" vs. "is-a", which have distinct semantics. A child is not a father, or a mother. Neither is a car an engine. Sorry to be pedantic about this, but using better examples would lead to better informed learners.

If you want to compare inheritance vs. composition, you need to introduce the notion of preferring abstractions or interfaces and dependency injection. Parent can be the interface that can "hasChild: Child". Similarly, MotorVehicle can be the interface that can "hasEngine: Engine". Instead of Person > Parent > Father | Mother and MotorVehicle > Car.

text:
I read most of this style guide a couple days ago and the part about auto is the one I tend to disagree with the most. I don't consider types to be of significant importance to understand code. The name of the variables and the name of the operations performed on these variables are significantly more important. Also, explicit typing can introduce unintended conversions and slicing. Explicit types are for member variables and function parameters. Every local variable shall be auto, IMO.
Also, requiring explicit typing tends to discourage people from using intermediate variables. This leading to longer nested expressions that, eventually, lead to a comment and to a more difficult debugging process (less variables to inspect, less locations to break on). Less expressions per line is more desirable to me than more explicit types.

The list of things you picked from the style guide is weird, your also not critical of any of these.

* spaces-vs-tabs is a meaningless debate things display differently in editors based on font and many other things, also there are many cases where displaying things different is desired with spaces this is not possible.

* in almost all cases it's going to be the safer option, you reduce implicit conversions in your example with widget I would trust the auto to have the correct type returned if you instead had "Widget" or "Button" I would be thinking is this slicing, constructing, converting what's happening.

* exceptions avoid the issue with unchecked returned values for errors, in your example the same thing with "g" not handling the exception can be said for "g" just ignoring the return value. also exceptions allow for better success code generation as your no longer littering your code with a bunch of conditional checks if each function returned successfully, their reason of existing API expectations is reasonable for not changing, but it's not a good reason to use it for all projects. Also single return path isn't the reason for no exceptions, with C++ and RAII single return path is no longer a thing which most people recommend, in fact it's sometimes nicer to have multiple return paths (within reason)

* your example of mother, father and child are broken, inheritance defines as "is-a" relationship so if you inherit from both mother and father then your saying a child is-a mother and also the child is-a father, then defining the attributes for both of those cases for the child, it's just not a reasonable view.  Instead a child has-a mother and has-a father in which case mother and father would be members of the child, you also completely switch the example to a car after so not showing an actual alternative. Abstract interfaces can still lead to a diamond problem however they make it more clear that they are interfaces and no the actual implementation of something.

I don't get the "bad inheritance" example. A child would NEVER inherit from either Mother nor Father, and it will EVEN NEVER-ER inheritj from BOTH

Inheritance models a "Is a" relationship. In your example you didn't seem to be aware of that basic principle about inheritance. But the example you gave implied that a child IS a Mother AND a Father which makes little sense regardless of coding style

Edit: That said, you even gave the solution in the video without properly developing it. Person should be an abstract class (Interface). And all 3: Mother, Father and Child should inherit from it. Then you could extend with composition. For example the Child in include a an instance of "Feedable" though which the Mother and the Father can feed the Child.

But then if you KNOW you will need to add features that apply to EVERY person (Maybe for this particular program every person should breath, and implementing that though composition of a "Lungs" object is kinda convoluted, instead you implement a Breath method directly in Person that calls itself every so often so that the person stays alive), THEN you could get away with some implementation inheritance. That way you don't have to manually give lungs to every person, which might lead to more concise and readable code! You have to be mindful of this tho. Since the moment a person that does NOT breath appears (For example a fish person, that would be killed by breathing air). Then you would have to do a lot of code rewriting. Since if you mindless let FishPerson inherit from Person. You might not even realize why all your Fish Persons are dead on arrival (A problem that would have not happened with composition. Since you would immediately realize that you should NOT give them regular Lungs, but instead some sort of "Water Lungs". Composition + Interface Inheritance is more redundant. But it is also more explicit, and as such leads to less unexpected behavior hidden in classes elsewhere in the project. While keeping the advantages of OOP)

author: @cruz1ale
text:
The example with Child inheriting from Mother and Father makes no sense. A class defines an object's identity, and inheritance is just a way to inherit parts of an identity from a different class. It doesn't have anything to do with objects inheriting from other objects. A Child cannot inherit both from a Father and a Mother, since a Child cannot _be_ both a Father and Mother.

A better example would've been to say that Child inherits from Person, but since a Mother is also someone's Child, the multiple inheritance scenario would be Mother inheriting both from Person and Child. But that's easily solved... there's no need to inherit from Person, since Child already inherits from Person.

author: @mathgeniuszach
text:
I've always heard terrible explanations as to why "inheritance is bad", and yours is... well it's better than the rest, but you still make the mistake in the diamond problem of extending two classes where it doesn't make sense to, i.e. a child is not both their father and mother, they have a father and mother, thus this is a bad example and composition would be clearly used. These bad examples were one of the reasons I never took these "arguments" seriously.

A better example is when modularity is involved. Say you want to create an object that is both a Sprite (has x and y coordinates and can be drawn), and is a Damagable (has hp and stats). Perhaps you may even want to change stats based on position and so interactions between both are necessary; changing one should change the other. Both of these make sense to have internal state to potentially inherit from. However, the diamond problem occurs here too.

There are still drawbacks to composition, like desynced state between child members. I always say to use what makes sense, don't pick something because you always did it that way.

author: @triularity
text:
If C++ developers just assume exceptions could be thrown by almost everything, and defensively code for that, then dealing with them generally isn't a problem. Of course, this is easier when done in a language which has them from the start (e.g. java), rather than after the fact. To help mitigate the problems, there is always the noexcept declaration (but only if using C++11 or later).. and even its design is broken since it doesn't prevent them indirectly bubbling up and pulling the rug out from the function. I think it would have been better for the compiler to require the function dealt with any potential exception to guarantee nothing (like you would with checked exceptions in java).

[For the record, I avoid using C++, unless I have too -- it's basically a dumpster fire of things piled on top of things, piled on top of things, over the decades and many revisions. With a new spec seemingly every year now, it's only getting worse (no mature language should be changing that often)]
